stories.body:
CEO behind Nvidia’s meteoric rise stepped down after it was revealed he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, then was reinstated days later

Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO of Nvidia , the company at the center of the AI boom, after leading it for more than 30 years. The announcement of his resignation came on 12 November. A week and a half later, he was reinstated as the chief executive in a unanimous vote by Nvidia’s board.

Huang, an electrical engineer by education, stewarded the company from a $1bn firm when it went public in 1999 to a company valued at more than $4tn in 2026. But in a matter of days, after it was revealed he had an extramarital affair with a woman that US officials believe to be a Chinese spy, Huang managed to wipe more than $600bn from the company’s valuation.

China has denied the accusations that it had tapped Alice Huang, the woman in question and a top executive at a datacenter company called Megaspeed, to be an intelligence asset, and called them a “smear”. US officials had reportedly started to monitor the Megaspeed executive after suspecting the firm was diverting powerful Nvidia AI chips to Chinese firms, in potential violation of export restrictions. The Biden and Trump administrations had prohibited US companies from exporting some of the more powerful AI chips to China over national security concerns.

Initially, it seemed that Huang’s ouster was unlikely, but in the days since he first disclosed an affair and affirmed his commitment to the company, the New York Times reported that there was a second affair – this time with another Nvidia executive. Reuters later reported a third affair, this one with another Nvidia employee.

How did we get here? Here’s a timeline of what we know about Huang’s entanglements.

2023

March 2023 Megaspeed, a datacenter firm, is spun out from a Chinese video game company

Megaspeed is the datacenter firm at the center of the spy allegations. Before it was its own company, it was a part of one of China’s largest video game companies, 7Road Holdings Ltd . At this time, Megaspeed was controlled by a firm called Huang Le Ltd, an entity affiliated with Alice Huang, according to Bloomberg.

November 2023 Megaspeed is sold to a Singaporean shell company and becomes an Nvidia cloud partner

Huang Le Ltd sells its shares of Megaspeed to a Singaporean shell company called Swiftdata. The sale comes weeks after Joe Biden issued an executive order limiting investment in China’s AI industry.

Soon after, Megaspeed is designated an Nvidia cloud partner, which means the company could get preferential access to Nvidia’s advanced AI chips.

2024

June 2024 Alice Huang and Jensen Huang are seen together in Taipei, Taiwan

Jensen Huang is seen with Alice Huang at a bar in Taipei where several AI industry executives had gathered . The person who introduced them to each other was Alice Huang’s husband , Kang Wei, who had worked with her on several business ventures, according to the Wall Street Journal.

2024 to 2025 Megaspeed receives hundreds of shipments of Nvidia AI chips

The Singapore-based firm fields 200 shipments of AI chips, according to the New York Times . The company then rents out compute power, which is fueled by these AI chips, to major companies including the Chinese firms Tencent and Alibaba.

September 2024 The US Department of Commerce begins investigating Megaspeed

The commerce department begins investigating whether Megaspeed is diverting Nvidia chips to Chinese firms, according to the New York Times. This could violate export restrictions on advanced AI chips.

2025

January 2025 Jensen Huang meets Donald Trump for the first time

Huang visits Donald Trump in the weeks after he takes office.

April 2025 Jensen Huang attends a dinner for donors at Mar-a-Lago

The dinner costs $1m a person and the president briefly puts a pause on imposing restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China. The restriction is ultimately implemented shortly after.

May 2025 Jensen Huang is again seen with Alice Huang

The two attend an industry conference in Taiwan. The New York Times also reports that Alice Huang visited the Nvidia headquarters in Santa Clara, California, two months earlier.

October 2025 Trump is reportedly briefed on the relationship between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang

The New York Times reports in October 2025 that intelligence officials told Trump that the two had a relationship and alleged that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Trump chose not to take action, according to the Times report. Trump has since said at a White House press conference that he didn’t remember being briefed on this.

December 2025 Trump approves the sale of more advanced Nvidia chips to China

Trump grants Nvidia permission to sell its second-most powerful chips to China. A portion of the sales would go to the US government.

2026

May 2026 Marco Rubio reportedly drafts a memo about Jensen Huang and Alice Huang

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, drafts the memo based on information gleaned from electronic surveillance of Alice Huang, according to the New York Times. The memo warns that Jensen Huang has become close to an alleged Chinese spy. Trump still invites Huang on his trip to China, saying in a social media post that he is honored to have “the Great Jensen Huang” on the trip.

October 2026 The New York Times reports Jensen Huang may have been targeted by a Chinese spy

At the time, Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo says Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang is nothing out of the ordinary.

8 November 2026 Jensen Huang admits to having an affair

In a letter to employees, Huang says that he had an extramarital affair, apologizes to his family and reaffirms his commitment to the company. The Nvidia board says it is investigating the relationship but has no reason to believe national security secrets or company secrets were divulged. “The board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate,” members of the Board say in a statement.

Silicon Valley leaders rally behind him , and at the time it appears that Huang might hang on to his job, despite his image being tarnished .

9 November 2026 Trump says he is ‘amazed’ by the allegations that Alice Huang is a spy

At a press conference , Trump says the FBI is investigating Jensen Huang but adds that he thinks Huang will be “in good shape”.

“And I asked him about that, and he … said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy,” the president says at a press conference. “I asked him that question: ‘Did you have any idea that she was a spy?’ He said: ‘I had no idea that she was a spy.’

“I really believe him,” Trump says.

10 November 2026 A shareholder in California files a lawsuit against Nvidia and its CEO

Retail investor Mark Kistenmacher files a lawsuit accusing the company of misleading investors over Huang’s affair, claiming that Nvidia did not disclose the situation and raised national security concerns that could threaten the company’s business prospects.

11 November 2026 The New York Times reports there was a second affair, and the Nvidia board reportedly prepares to oust Huang

The New York Times reports that Huang also allegedly had an affair with the company’s vice-president of healthcare.

At this point things are looking precarious for Jensen Huang, and then the Wall Street Journal reports that the Nvidia board is preparing to oust the CEO.

12 November 2026 Jensen Huang steps down as CEO of Nvidia

Huang steps down, effectively ending his 33-year tenure leading the company he co-founded in 1993. The board starts a search for the company’s next CEO while the company’s chief finance officer, Colette Kress, serves as interim CEO.

Meanwhile, shares in the company continue to plummet.

17 November 2026 Nvidia’s board says it will not reinstate Jensen Huang

Nvidia “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”, the chair of the company’s board says. Harvey Jones makes the remark during Nvidia’s first quarterly earnings report since Huang’s ouster.

Nvidia announces the same day that its quarterly revenue beat expectations, coming in at $115.84bn, doubling from the same time period a year ago.

23 November 2026 Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia’s CEO

Nvidia reinstates Huang as chief executive in a stunning reversal. The company’s shares surge on the news, jumping 33% and adding more than $1tn to its market value.

Donald Trump, who had called for Huang’s return, trumpets his own involvement in negotiations with Nvidia’s board to return the former CEO to his position. The president says, “the country needs Jensen’s leadership” and that the US government has no “evidence that [Huang] has engaged in any unlawful conduct”.

In a statement , the board says it “believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers”.

stories.title: Trump halts Iowa detonation, says new governor to blame if it blows accidentally
stories.summary: The Army said on Sunday that it would carry out the detonation on Wednesday.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The Army said on Sunday that it would carry out the detonation on Wednesday.

President Trump took to social media Monday afternoon to announce that he has ordered the US military to halt plans to detonate 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide at an Army ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa. Trump claimed that the fate of the unstable, highly explosive material is now in the hands of a federal court and Rob Sand, Iowa’s governor-elect, who won’t be sworn into office until January.

The Army had planned to detonate the barrels on November 20, but delayed the blast on Thursday amid public outcry and a legal challenge from environmental groups. The explosion will launch a plume of toxic gases and neurotoxic lead that could reach up to 100 miles away from the Iowa facility, the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP).

Iowa residents and officials said they learned of the detonation only days beforehand. The environmental groups, led by Earthjustice, claimed in an emergency court filing that the Army had not fully considered safer options for disposing of the lead azide before planning the detonation.

Late Thursday, a federal appeals court granted Earthjustice’s request to put a hold on the Army’s permit from the Environmental Protection Agency, which allowed for the controlled detonation to be carried out. Around the same time, Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said the detonation would be postponed until Monday so the military could communicate with Iowans about the situation and plans.

Lead azide risk

Documents released by the Army last week said that the military first learned in March that the lead azide had started to degrade and crystallize. Lead azide is used in detonators for munitions, but in crystallized form it becomes highly unstable and sensitive to physical movement or friction. The IAAAP is said to contain around 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons) of lead azide in barrels held in earth-covered containers.

In late March, the Army awarded a contract to MuniRem Environmental, a Georgia-based firm that uses chemicals to neutralize munitions to safely dispose of the lead azide, according to a New York Times report . MuniRem uses a sulfur-based solution that reportedly breaks down explosives and immobilizes toxic chemicals, eliminating the need for detonation. The company had proposed spraying the inside of the earth-covered containers housing the barrels as well as the barrel surfaces to neutralize risks of spontaneous explosions.

But two months later, the Army canceled the contract without explanation. An Army contracting officer told MuniRem in an email at the time that the cancellation “was not based on deficiencies” in MuniRem’s plans, the Times reported. The company’s founder said MuniRem filed public records requests to get more information on why the contract was scrapped, but it has not received a response

Now, the Army claims that the lead azide has only degraded further since March and it cannot move the barrels or even open their lids without risking a catastrophic explosion. Further, it claims that winter temperatures in the coming days increase the risk of spontaneous detonation.

Imminent threat

“As the temperatures drop, the risk of an uncontrolled explosion increases because the formed crystals can break more easily in freezing temperatures,” lawyers for the Trump administration wrote in a court filing over the weekend . “If the crystals break, this could cause a chain reaction detonation that could cause an uncontrolled dispersal of lead azide into the environment.”

The Army claims that the only choice now is between a controlled, mitigated explosion or an uncontrolled, unmitigated explosion. In court filings this weekend, government lawyers argued that the Army does not need the now-suspended EPA permit to move forward with the detonation, because the Army has determined that the lead azide poses an “immediate threat to human health, public safety, property, or the environment.”

Last Thursday, Telle said that the delay until Monday was the “latest possible moment” for a controlled detonation before temperatures dropped dangerously low. But the military subsequently delayed the detonation again until Tuesday and then pushed it back to Wednesday .

In his social media post Monday, Trump said he thought carrying out the controlled detonation was the “proper course.” But he said he was making the decision the responsibility of the federal appeals court and Governor-elect Rob Sand, a Democrat. If the lead azide spontaneously detonates on their watch, Trump claimed, they will be fully to blame.

“If he or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation,” Trump wrote.

In a social media post Sunday evening, Sand called for answers on how the situation was able to become so dangerous, specifically raising the question of why MuniRem’s contact was canceled.

“Iowans deserve transparency over how we got here, then answers and accountability to stop this from ever happening again,” he wrote.

stories.title: Trump faces backlash after saying he 'convinced' Nvidia to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang
stories.summary: Nvidia had come under pressure from President Trump to reappoint Huang, whose comeback helped add $1tn to the company's stock value.

A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to Nvidia

Published 23 November 2026

Nvidia has reinstated CEO Jensen Huang just days after rejecting his offer to return to the AI chipmaker - and less than two weeks after he was forced to resign over a reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

The company came under pressure by Donald Trump to reappoint Huang - and on Monday, the US president said he "made the deal" to "convince" the tech giant's board to bring him back.

But now both Trump and Nvidia are facing bipartisan backlash from lawmakers, just as Huang is due to testify before Congress next week.

The CEO's comeback helped end a week-long losing streak in US stocks that left the S&P 500 in correction territory, and added nearly $1 trillion to Nvidia's market value.

Stock prices for Nvidia fell sharply after Huang stepped down, but jumped by 31% after he was reappointed on Monday - adding about $1tn to the company's market value.

But Nvidia's closing price was still down slightly from its Friday morning opening price.

As Asian stock markets opened, Nvidia racked up more gains and helped lift other share prices across the tech sector.

Asia markets jump as Nvidia boss Jensen Huang reinstated after spy scandal

This video can not be played

Watch: Nvidia's stock skyrockets after Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO

Board Chairman Harvey C Jones said in a statement earlier in the day: "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers."

The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.

It was only last Tuesday that the board explicitly said it did not intend to reinstate him.

Huang resigned from Nvidia on 12 November following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman, Alice Huang, who was alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence.

On Monday, the US Commerce Department announced it was preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer where Alice Huang was CEO.

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO

In a brief interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump said he had spoken to Nvidia's board of directors and "convinced" them to bring back Huang. Trump praised the Nvidia board for acting "really responsibly" in reinstating the CEO.

"They did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump said. "And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot."

"People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it's a threat to lose him," the president added.

The president was asked whether Nvidia stock losses after Huang resigned last week had influenced his decision to personally intervene.

"Probably so," Trump said.

The rise and fall and rise again of Jensen Huang Published 12 hours ago

How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy? Published 12 hours ago

Congress vows to investigate Nvidia and the Trump administration's role

The head of the International Association for Safe and Ethical AI told the BBC that the Nvidia board must have been under "enormous pressure" from the White House to reinstate Huang.

Prof Stuart Russell, who is professor of computer science at UC Berkeley, said the stock price of Nvidia and similar firms has been a major factor in "underpinning US economic growth for years".

"I assume the White House was worried that the markets would go down a lot further in the next few weeks unless they go him back in," he says.

Trump's vocal backing of Huang comes despite the concerns of US lawmakers, including some Republicans, over the CEO's affair and Nvidia's compliance with US export controls.

Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to lead the House of Representatives as Speaker when Democrats take control in January called the decision to reinstate Huang "indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible" and vowed that Congress will conduct "a swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation".

"We will not allow America's national security to be sold out by the Trump Administration for personal financial gain," he said, echoing many lawmakers on Monday who said that Congress must pass strong export control legislation.

Huang is scheduled to appear before Congress for a closed-door interview with three House committees on 1 December. Two days later, he has been asked to testify before the Senate banking committee.

Senator Elizabeth Warren, who is set to be chairwoman of the Senate Banking Committee once Democrats take control of the chamber in January, said in a statement that the reinstatement was "reckless".

"The Trump Administration also needs to explain to Congress what 'input' was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement," she also said.

Republicans, too, called for answers.

"Nvidia should have moved on without Huang and ignored the administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang," said Republican Representative Don Bacon, who chairs a House subcommittee on cyber security.

"We cannot say we want to win the AI race and then give China our best technology. We need sunlight on who is responsible."

The chair of the Senate's select committee on intelligence, Republican Tom Cotton said: "The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back."

Nvidia value climbs by almost $1tn and tech stocks rally after Jensen Huang returns Published 7 hours ago

Faisal Islam: Why Jensen Huang proved too big to fire Published 11 hours ago

US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal Published 5 hours ago

Trump's personal Nvidia investments

Since returning last year to the White House, Trump has amassed a significant level of investment in Nvidia. Recent financial disclosures show he purchased $265,000 in its stock and sold as much as $15,000 worth of shares in September.

A BBC review of his government financial disclosures for the last two years shows he purchased shares of Nvidia stock worth between $23m and $86m (£18m and £66m). And he has bought Nvidia stock 85 separate times through a number of investment accounts.

The value of those holdings would have been affected by the recent fall in Nvidia's stock price amid Huang's exit.

Trump has also sold some of his stake in Nvidia since returning to the presidency. Over 19 sales, Trump gained between $3.5m and $10.2m, according to his government disclosures.

The BBC has contacted the White House.

Both Trump and White House have repeatedly rejected assertions that he has profited from the presidency. The president has said "everybody" was making money from rising stocks and he does not make decisions related to his investment accounts.

The White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons.

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Accused official leaked national secrets to unnamed country and received payments worth over $150,000, state-linked publisher says

A Chinese official has been sentenced to death for spying for a foreign country, a government-linked publisher has said.

Gold Wall Press, a publishing company associated with China’s national administration of state secrets protection, said the convicted person was surnamed Ma and was approached and recruited by an unnamed foreign intelligence service while working abroad.

Chinese courts typically do not publish information about state security cases, but in recent years the powerful ministry of state security and Gold Wall Press have increasingly publicised arrests, as well as using social media, movies and comics to promote warnings about espionage.

The statement on Monday said Ma had signed a cooperation agreement containing clauses on “confidentiality” and “loyalty” and received fixed monthly payments. In total, it said, he provided 35 pieces of information that were classified as national secrets and received payments worth more than 1m yuan ($150,000).

An intelligence operative identified as Kailin “frequently arranged to meet with Ma, hoping to engage with him more”, citing an interest in learning Chinese, the statement said. Kailin later introduced him to a colleague who threatened to report his earlier disclosures to Chinese authorities if he refused to cooperate.

After returning to China, Ma continued to gather intelligence for the foreign agency, which provided him with a laptop, the statement said. He used his position to collect material from classified documents during the day and transmitted it overseas at night via an espionage website.

The statement did not identify the countries involved, or say when or where he was sentenced or whether he had already been executed.

The case comes as US intelligence has been publicising its own efforts to recruit sources in China. The five most-viewed videos on the CIA’s YouTube channel are recruiting advertisements in Mandarin.

“This shocking case serves as yet another wake-up call,” the Gold Wall Press said, warning that foreign intelligence agencies were “cunning” and used emotional ties, financial interests and threats to recruit people in key positions.

The statement also urged officials to remain vigilant, strengthen their loyalty to the Communist party, protect state secrets and guard against foreign recruitment.

In 2023 Beijing broadened its anti-espionage law, expanding the definition of espionage and strengthening the investigative powers of state security authorities. The following year it revised its state secrets law to extend restrictions on sensitive information to so-called “work secrets”.

stories.title: No 10 North will face greater scrutiny as Burnham's 10-year plan looms
stories.summary: The work of Number 10 North in Manchester has been kept largely away from the headlines since it opened in July.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 4 hours ago

The work of Andy Burnham's new Number 10 North office in Manchester has been kept largely away from the headlines since it opened in July.

But the officials based there are mainly focused on two soon-to-be-published documents that could go on to define his time as prime minister.

The first is Burnham's 10-year plan, which is due next month, and which the prime minister says will lay out a path "to where I believe we all want Britain to be".

The second is the 'rewiring the state' white paper, a detailed policy document that will follow in the new year and should give the clearest indication yet of what power Burnham hopes to move away from Westminster to other parts of the country.

But despite Burnham insisting his new Manchester team will be the "engine room" of change, others in government question how much difference they can really make.

There's talk among Labour MPs that the 10-year plan, which has also had significant input from Westminster departments, will not go as far as the prime minister had hoped.

But one official who has seen elements of the plan said it will be "pretty weighty" and include "quite a lot of radicalism".

Number 10 North has been focused on how the plan can deliver on Burnham's pledge to achieve "growth in every postcode".

One major theme is expected to be reindustrialisation, with advisers exploring how to attract businesses to less prosperous towns and cities.

Staff in Manchester are also said to be looking at what parts of the country may not see growth through reindustrialisation – such as some rural and coastal areas – and what the alternative offer for those places could be.

Eyebrows were raised in Whitehall this summer when a government statement said that "local economic growth policy" would be transferred "from HM Treasury directly into No 10 North".

Some saw that as an attempt to disempower the Treasury, but sources there insist that no serious decisions on growth can be made without the department's involvement and approval.

Burnham's Number 10 North goes on multi-million pound hiring spree Published 30 October

'Mindset shift' needed within government on No10 North, says deputy Published 21 October

When Burnham first announced plans for the Manchester base, he singled out housing as an issue on which it would take the lead.

In a speech last month Number 10 North's deputy director highlighted health, transport and education as other areas it was focused on.

While it's understood the 10-year plan is likely to include long-term ambitions for social care, skills training and council housebuilding, there are doubts within government departments about exactly how involved Number 10 North will eventually be in those areas.

One Whitehall official said "most things" that have been announced as Number 10 North priorities have in practice "stayed with other departments".

They said Number 10 North is "not doing delivery" because it "doesn't have its own resource" and is "underpowered compared to departments" in London.

A recent hiring spree will see around 120 officials and advisers working from Number 10 North when it moves into its permanent premises next spring.

That is almost half of the around 280 staff members that work for "Number 10 South", a term some advisers are now using for Downing Street.

But even those staffing levels are only a fraction of the numbers employed by other departments.

The Treasury's north of England campus in Darlington, which was set up in 2021, has around 3,000 staff.

John Healey is said to have been particularly impressed with the Darlington campus's record of hiring people who would otherwise not have joined the civil service, something Downing Street hopes to achieve in Manchester too.

Darlington's most senior civil servant, Beth Russell, has been working with Number 10 North to share her experience of how best to set up a new government office outside London.

Prime ministers have for decades been frustrated by how little power Number 10 can sometimes wield within Whitehall, arguing that levers can be pulled but nothing then happens.

One question at the heart of the Number 10 North project is whether it will eventually wield genuine power itself or merely decide which powers to take from Westminster and give to mayors and other regional politicians around the country.

A government source said Number 10 North's current role is "more in convening" people from elsewhere and argued the prime minister would need to choose what he wanted it to do in the future.

They added: "I could see it going two different ways.

"Will it be more delivery or will it be more in the conventional role of Number 10?

"Maybe it's not best placed to do things, but maybe directing and convening are also important things to do."

In July Burnham chaired the first meeting of the National Economic Council at No 10 North, bringing together ministers and regional mayors

Regional mayors have been regular visitors of Number 10 North and are set to be earmarked for much more expansive powers in the 'rewiring the state' white paper.

England currently has 14 metro mayors, a number which is likely to be expanded in the coming years.

Sources in both Number 10 and the Treasury say "fiscal devolution" will be a major part of the Burnham agenda.

People close to the prime minister say that is likely to ultimately mean more cash-raising, spending and borrowing power for mayors.

Two of Burnham's early announcements this summer saw mayors given a share of income tax and the ability to introduce a tourist tax for people visiting their areas.

The Treasury believes one of the most underreported elements of Healey's Budget last month was a £1.5bn borrowing facility that will be given to mayors from 2028.

Sources say that in the future projects such as Doncaster-Sheffield Airport, which Healey gave his backing to, could be given the financial go-ahead directly by mayors, without the need for a separate thumbs up from the chancellor.

For now mayors have each been asked to submit a list of projects to Number 10 North, which they feel are being held up by government processes.

Government departments in Westminster have also been asked to identify what areas they are currently responsible for which could potentially be devolved to mayors and other local government officials.

What's less clear is how the prime minister's devolution plans will affect Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland and whether he is keen for them too to adopt a mayoral model.

At a recent meeting in Glasgow, Burnham said he would discuss that further with the leaders of the devolved nations.

He recently rejected a proposal from the First Minister of Wales to devolve more responsibilities over policing and justice.

Away from the gaze of backbench MPs, opposition parties and Westminster journalists, Number 10 North has so far been able to go about its business without drawing much attention.

But as Burnham's long-term plans for the country start to become more clear, the scrutiny faced by his Manchester power base is likely to grow too.

stories.title: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO, board chair
stories.summary: Trump says he spoke to the board and that Huang "did nothing wrong."
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Trump says he spoke to the board and that Huang “did nothing wrong.”

Originally published November 23, 2026

Nvidia’s board of directors has voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO and chairman of the board, just 11 days after he resigned in the wake of multiple scandals .

The reinstatement, announced Monday morning , is “effective immediately” and was based in part on “input from senior levels of the United States government” that assured the board members that “Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

That assurance comes despite Huang’s admitted affair with a woman who, US intelligence sources believe, was working as a Chinese spy and allegations that Nvidia had subverted export controls meant to keep Nvidia chips from reaching China. It also comes despite multiple developing investigations from multiple different government departments into those and other alleged national security, accounting, and corporate governance failures.

Huang had been seeking a return to Nvidia since shortly after his resignation, reportedly forming a war room to strategize how best to bring it to pass. Last week, Huang posted on social media that “if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

President Trump has also been a major backer of Huang’s return to Nvidia. “I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang,” he wrote on Truth Social last week. “It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A.” In a social media post immediately following the reinstatement, Trump called it “the correct and proper decision” and confirmed that “the United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.”

Appearing on CNBC Monday morning , Trump said that he had spoken to the Nvidia board “directly and indirectly” about Huang’s reinstatement, and that Huang “did nothing wrong.” Losing “the brainpower of someone like [Huang]” would be “a much bigger threat” than anything related to his alleged interactions with China, Trump said.

“We’ve done a very thorough investigation and the investigation showed that… he had bad judgement having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents,” Trump said. “You have to protect our geniuses and there aren’t enough of them.”

We’ll be right back after this brief interruption

Huang’s tenure at Nvidia dates back to the company’s founding in 1993, when he and three cofounders were focused on the then-nascent field of GPU hardware aimed at PC gamers. In the decades since, the highly parallel cores in those GPUs have been embraced first by cryptocurrency miners and then AI companies, propelling the company to its position as the most valuable in the world at its October peak.

Nvidia stock—the price of which had sunk roughly 25 percent since Huang’s resignation was announced and nearly 50 percent since its peak—was up about 30 percent in early morning trading in the immediate aftermath of Huang’s reinstatement announcement.

Huang’s return echoes, in some ways, that of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who was fired almost exactly three years ago after the board said it “no longer has confidence in his ability to continue leading OpenAI.” Two weeks later, Altman was back at the helm after many employees threatened a mass revolt and departure if he wasn’t brought back.

In Huang’s case, the revolt following his departure came not from employees but from fellow titans of the tech industry. Executives including Altman, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, xAI’s Elon Musk and Anduril’s Palmer Luckey are among the prominent industry figures who have publicly offered him support in the days since his resignation.

In its statement, the Nvidia board reiterated that it has retained independent counsel and formed a committee of independent directors to investigate what it calls Huang’s targeting by “a foreign intelligence effort.” The company has also formed a National Security and Export Control Committee to “oversee trade compliance and national security risks,” and is seeking to hire a new chief compliance officer.

stories.title: The catch in IBM’s offer to relocate its U.S.-based immigrant workers
stories.summary: Ending U.S. visa sponsorship and shifting roles abroad helps the company retain talent, but leaves employees paying a steep financial and personal price.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Tech Giants

Ending U.S. visa sponsorship and shifting roles abroad helps the company retain talent, but leaves employees paying a steep financial and personal price.

For some IBM employees, keeping their jobs could mean moving to another country — and taking a steep pay cut in the process.

Earlier this month, IBM said it would no longer support the U.S. immigration status of workers in its consulting division, offering them the option to take a role with the company in another country or exit, according to a Bloomberg report citing a company document.

“IBM Consulting participates in U.S. high-skilled visa programs to address skill shortages,” an IBM spokesperson told Rest of World . “That participation has been declining for a number of years, and as skill availability and client need have evolved, we have opted to discontinue visa and green card sponsorship for the majority of such roles in IBM Consulting.”

IBM Consulting employs more than 150,000 people globally. The company does not disclose the geographical split for its workforce, making it hard to ascertain the exact number of workers impacted by this decision. On November 19, the company’s career portal listed 1,278 open roles for the consulting division outside the U.S., including 1,125 in India, 23 in Singapore, and 18 in the U.K. In the U.S., it listed 89 roles.

For employees, relocation does not automatically ensure continued engagement, effective collaboration, or equal access to professional opportunities, Zakaria Laaraj, founder of consultancy Global New Ventures, told Rest of World . It may affect their access to decision-makers, established networks, and career opportunities. “The credibility of such an offer depends on employee tenure, available positions, immigration requirements, and compensation,” Laaraj said.

Discussions on Blind, an anonymous employee forum used by 14 million professionals, suggest relocating may not be realistic for many.

Moving to India, for instance, could mean an approximately 80% pay cut, one IBM employee wrote on Blind.

“Employees get three weeks to decide,” Blind’s CEO Sunguk Moon told Rest of World . “The alternative is three months of severance and a last day of December 31. And the news came in a surprise one-on-one ‘career sync’ with a manager.”

For any relocation option to be viable, companies must go beyond just assigning a new job to their employee, George Carrillo, CEO of career development and staffing company HireMe, told Rest of World .

Moving a position can mean uprooting a family.” George Carrillo, CEO of and staffing company HireMe

“Moving a position can mean uprooting a family. It affects a spouse’s employment, children’s schooling, healthcare, and years of planning. HR should provide clear options, deadlines, and coordinated support. Leaders must own the follow-through,” Carrillo said.

Most U.S. tech giants are navigating the challenges arising from changing visa norms under Donald Trump’s leadership.

“IBM has an advantage because it already operates international offices with the infrastructure and staff to absorb those workers,” Lacey Kaelani, CEO of job search engine Metaintro, told Rest of World . “Rather than abandoning the talent, companies like IBM can move the work to where the talent is.”

Earlier this year, Amazon allowed stranded H-1B workers to work from India amid consular delays but only temporarily. Microsoft defended its international talent hiring strategy in an October blog post pushing back against the U.S. administration’s allegations that it replaces American workers with foreign visa holders. The statement followed its suspension from the Department of Labor’s PERM green card program alongside Adobe and six other IT outsourcing firms, including TCS and Infosys.

“Companies are looking for solutions, but they’re also making business decisions,” Cassandra Fultz, co-founder of Doherty Fultz Immigration, told Rest of World . “Sponsoring an employee indefinitely, particularly when the outcome is uncertain, can be expensive and disruptive. Moving that employee to an existing operation abroad may be an option with more stability for the business. That doesn’t mean every employee will be offered the opportunity for placement abroad. Each country has its own eligibility requirements and work authorization rules. Companies will inevitably prioritize the people and positions they consider most valuable or difficult to replace.”

Even employees are reevaluating the lure of the American Dream as the uncertainty tax of constant visa changes weighs heavily on them. The wait for green cards for Indian nationals — who typically receive three-quarters of the H-1B visas and comprise the majority of the green card queue — can take several decades, according to the National Foundation for American Policy . Even with Democrats winning control of both the House and the Senate, immigration issues will stay with the White House and executive agencies.

“Mid-career professionals in the queue for green cards are most impacted,” Abhijit Bhaduri, former general manager for global learning and development at Microsoft and author of the upcoming book AIdentity: How to Become Irreplaceable in the New World of Work , told Rest of World . “They built a life in a country that still lists them as temporary. A visa is a document. But the vanishing green card queue feels like a broken promise. They followed every rule for years, and the finish line moved. You can relocate a job overnight. Rebuilding and redesigning a new identity takes years. That is the invisible price that gets missed.”

How Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia impacts China’s AI supply chain

The founder’s stunning departure removes Beijing’s biggest advocate in Silicon Valley, accelerates chip stockpiling, and leaves Asian suppliers bracing for what comes next.

A rare strike in Taiwan exposes labor unrest beneath the global AI rush

Labor disputes and unionization in Taiwan’s semiconductor industry highlight growing worker discontent over the unequal distribution of profits from the AI boom.

stories.title: Chris Mason: Can Burnham turn volume down on EU debate?
stories.summary: The BBC's Chris Mason analyses what the EU conversation means for Labour and the PM.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 4 hours ago

When the prime minister told MPs "there will be no banging on about Europe" from him, my mind flashed back 20 years.

It is 2006 and a fresh faced David Cameron had just taken over as the Conservative leader , promising, yes you guessed it, to stop "banging on" about Europe.

And we all know how that turned out: a decade later as prime minister, he held and lost a referendum on whether the UK should stay in the European Union, as he advocated, or leave.

Andy Burnham's address to the Commons, after Friday's EU-UK Summit in Brussels, felt like an attempt by a man who chose to turn the Europe conversation up to full blast this autumn, to try to turn the volume back down again.

All of this prompts two big questions: whether he will be able to do that and what, in the end, Labour promises at the next general election.

Asked if that could include seeking a mandate for another in/out referendum at that election, he didn't rule that out.

"If it's in Britain's national interest, I will recommend it to this House. If it is not, then I won't," he said.

But he very carefully left his options open: "There is no fixed opinion here. There is no fixed destination."

So he might offer a referendum. Or he might not.

My approach to EU is pragmatic, says Burnham Published 9 hours ago

He also suggested the frequency of his public utterances on the subject may be limited, insisting there would be no "running commentary," offering instead what he called "a calm, constructive and pragmatic consideration of what is in Britain's interest in the long term."

Plus, he said Europe could change in the coming years. A nod, without naming her, that Marine Le Pen could become president of France, for instance. How might that shift the debate?

Burnham's willingness to repeatedly talk about the European question in the last few months has, inevitably, spawned quite the reaction.

A campaign group, Stay Out, has got itself up and running to argue exactly that.

And the European Movement is helping launch a rival outfit called, again, you guessed it, Get In.

It is a reminder that that the EU question has a knack of getting under the skin of British politics, often to the exclusion of other things, sometimes to the exclusion of seemingly everything.

Can the prime minister successfully manage the volume switch so the topic is background hubbub in 2027, rather than a deafening din?

Ursula von der Leyen, Andy Burnham and António Costa at the EU-UK Summit in Brussels last week.

Meanwhile, what does the European Union itself make of all of this? EU sources see Andy Burnham's desire to "brainstorm" with them what the future relationship might look like as "normal diplomacy" as one figure put it, adding: "I don't think there are many options. And they are clear. The status quo. The customs union. The single market. And full membership."

They mirror his expectation that "brainstorming" won't involve additional meetings, let alone a structured set of bespoke talks arriving at a conclusion. "We don't need a template. It will be part of the regular discussion," is how it was put to me.

On Thursday, the government will publish its European Partnerships Bill, the legislation needed to enact, at the UK end, the agreements reached at the summit. Also later this week, the legal text of those agreements is due to be published – the small print of which will be pored over.

How much might the UK have to compensate the EU for, for instance, if a future government were to decide to reverse the changes that have just been signed up to? Within the deal it is expected that were Britain to change its mind on the food export part of the deal in the next 10 years, Brussels would charge London for the reinstallation of the checkpoints that will soon no longer be needed.

Then, there are the ongoing negotiations between the two sides about unresolved areas of potential cooperation. The EU has made much of its desire to secure a deal on university tuition fees in the next six months, with the hope that EU students will pay no more at UK universities than British students do. The deal would be reciprocal for UK students studying elsewhere in Europe. Both sides think an agreement is within reach. Senior figures in Whitehall are also encouraged by the EU's willingness to include the UK in its 'Made in Europe' plan to protect European industry from China. Then there is the EU's common electricity market.

But even if all these things are agreed – and they will all provoke debate here about whether or not they are good ideas – Andy Burnham has publicly said incremental changes only take the UK so far.

It is clear he has an appetite and an interest in going further. The question, ultimately, is how much further?

stories.title: EFF to Congress: Mass Surveillance Is Too Important to Shove into Must-Pass Bill
stories.summary: In June 2026, the surveillance authority Section 702 of FISA expired absent a consensus among lawmakers over the terms of its reauthorization . Now, with the program set to truly turn off within the next few months, surveillance hawks and national security maximalists are rushing to renew this secretive power by shoving it into a must-pass bill, like a continuing resolution to fund the government or the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) or an end of year, rushed, funding bill to prevent a shutdown. This would be both undemocratic and suppress any real chance at reform. In an effort to prevent that, EFF has singed into a letter with over 25 civil liberties organizations, including the ACLU, Color of Change, and the Brennan Center, to urge Congress not to allow such a significant and dangerous program to be tacked onto a must-pass bill. The letter says: “The NDAA is among the most important bills Congress considers each year. It should not be used as a vehicle to circumvent or to cut short this long-running bipartisan debate over Americans’ civil liberties and constitutional rights, nor to force lawmakers to choose between supporting our national defense and ending warrantless spying on Americans. Adding language in the NDAA conference to reauthorize Section 702 that has not been fully debated and voted on would be a serious procedural and substantive failure, and a betrayal of the democratic process.” You can read the entire letter here . Section 702 grants the government authority to compel a telecommunications company to hand over data to the National Security Agency (NSA) in an attempt to protect national security by monitoring communications overseas—but this is only a piece of what the law does. Because we live in a globalized world, communications between people in other countries and in the United States often gets hoovered up. stories.summary: It's been a tough couple of weeks for anyone trying to use email , fly , spend money , use an Apple device *, or do signals intelligence . Technical service outages are nothing new, but why do so many big ones seem to be happening all at once? Are hackers, AI, and international conflicts to blame? And what can we do about it? Since most service interruptions don't make the news, it's hard to get a baseline on how often we see them happen normally. But after a major incident like the Microsoft cloud outage on November 12 , any smaller disruption is more likely to become a story as part of a pattern instead of an isolated incident. We would have heard plenty about the Air Traffic Control problems anyway, but the November 18 disruption to the PlayStation Network might have gotten less attention. There might appear to be a spike or an upward trend in outages, but we can't easily verify that, and the increased coverage will tend to make it seem more significant and interconnected than it necessarily is regardless. One boring reason we might see an uptick in problems right now is the date on the calendar. With Thanksgiving travel, Black Friday, Cyber Monday, Giving Tuesday, and Surveillance Sunday (we assume) all coming up, organizations often schedule major system updates for the first three weeks of November. This helps them prepare for holiday traffic, and lets them shift the outage risk to the time before those dates when they may consider it far more important to maintain reliable service. While none of these particular outages have yet been directly attributed to AI ( or to malicious hackers ), bank CEOs and the NSA briefed congress and reportedly attributed at least some of them to rushed attempts to patch vulnerabilities found by AI. That’s understandable: all software updates carry risk, and companies and governments are having to deploy more updates, and faster, than they’ve ever needed to before. stories.body:
Sheepdog trials don’t always take place in a field. Some take place in a pub.

Across New Zealand, “bark-ups” are a common sight at pubs and agricultural events, and feature a home-bred invention: the New Zealand huntaway dog breed. The aim of the bark-up is simple: find the dog with the best bark.

To outsiders, the spectacle raises an obvious question: why would anyone hold a competition to find the sheepdog that barks the loudest? The answer lies not just in the sheep stations of New Zealand where the huntaway was developed, but in the colonisation of New Zealand, for sheepdogs are breeds of empire. It’s something I explore in my new book .

The modern sheepdog was a Victorian invention. Queen Victoria herself was a fan of the collie , buying the best from shepherds on the England-Scotland borders. Those shepherds were at the helm of the emerging sheepdog trialling scene at the start of the 20th century.

In the process, sheepdogs came to embody Victorian moral values. The ideal dog displayed discipline, intelligence, restraint, obedience and industriousness, and perhaps most of all, silence while working – qualities that were equally applicable to the shepherd.

Organisations such as the International Sheep Dog Society reinforced these ideals. Under its influential honorary secretary, James Reid, the border collie was invented not merely as a useful farm dog but as the pinnacle of canine improvement.

Exported throughout Britain’s settler colonies, it became a breed of empire, carrying with it particular ideas about good stockmanship, moral character and agricultural modernity. Reid went so far as to describe the sheepdog as the foundation of the pastoral economy, whose intelligence and labour underpinned the success of the British empire.

Scottish settlers had already taken their sheepdogs to New Zealand in the mid-19th Century. But it would be a Northumbrian, James Lilico, who would transform New Zealand’s sheepdogs. Arriving in 1894 to work as a shepherd, he immediately sent home for his dog Captain, disappointed by the “useless mongrels” he had been given to work.

So started half a century of importing the finest sheepdogs he could source, usually championship winning trial dogs, earning him the title of the “collie king of New Zealand”. Lilico imported sheepdogs that had been bred with the quality known as “eye” (herding using an intense stare) that had become highly valued among triallists. Breeding them, Lilico championed the superiority of what he called “border dogs” in his weekly column in the New Zealand Farmer periodical.

Lilico’s actions were not universally welcomed, in particular his criticism of the sheepdogs and shepherds who worked New Zealand’s high country. For the shepherds of these regions, Lilico’s strong-eyed dogs were too slow, too delicate and insufficiently forceful. In their view, sheep needed to be moved, not mesmerised.

Their alternative was the huntaway. What marked out the huntaway from the border collie was its noise. Without fences and across wide open country, noise had become a valuable tool for shepherds. Before setting out to muster sheep, shepherds gathered their dogs and instructed them to bark. This bark up – just like those now seen in pubs – guided sheep from a distance, so by the time shepherds arrived the sheep were already on the move.

Read more: Your dog may be wilder than you think, according to canine sleep research

If its bark united the huntaway, their appearance did anything but. Old photographs reveal a variety of different appearances and types: from small and fluffy to larger looking collies. But as sheep farming expanded from the South Island into the hill country of the North Island, the huntaway began to evolve.

To make the huntaway more powerful to deal with stubborn Romney sheep , its voice got louder. Breeding experiments involving mastiff, rottweiler, labrador, hound and other breeds sought to improve its barking power. A bigger huntaway became more common, but even now the huntaway defies standardisation beyond its capacity to bark all day.

Crucially, while the development of New Zealand agriculture was part of a scientific “grasslands revolution” , these scientists had little to do with sheepdogs. The huntaway instead reflected the spirit of farmers, as a “practical dog for practical men”. Scientists and breed societies were kept well away in fear of ruining the dog.

Recognition and uncertainty

In 2013 the huntaway was recognised as a unique breed by the New Zealand Kennel Club, but its origins were still uncertain. Recent genetic studies show that it is related to the border collie, and other breeds imported in the 19th century. Genetic traces of the breeds used for power are harder to find, reinforcing the mythology that surrounds the breed.

It may also be that its defining feature – the bark – is not simply a New Zealand invention but an echo of its past. Back in Scotland in 1935, James Reid had given a lecture celebrating the border collie conquering all other breeds of sheepdog. Its popularity had meant that other barking sheepdogs used across Wales and southern England had no place, consigning them to history.

When James Lilico wrote about the huntaway in one of his three books, he received a letter from a shepherd in north Wales suggesting that the Huntaway sounded no different to the dog known as ci hanos , a dog that used noise to drive sheep onto the hills in the springtime.

Lilico had planned on importing one of these as part of a breeding experiment. Such an experiment might be more valuable today as the huntaway gene pool narrows: the closure of large sheep stations in New Zealand is making breeding selection a challenge. In doing so, it raises existential questions about sheepdogs themselves, because without sheep there will be no sheepdogs.

stories.body:
At the Commonwealth summit in Antigua in November 2026, Britain’s King Charles expressed sorrow for Britain’s role in the slave trade.

Days earlier, UK prime minister Andy Burnham said Britain was open to a formal apology but ruled out financial reparations. Ghana’s president, John Mahama, replied that dialogue must go beyond an apology to reparatory justice.

The exchange neatly captures the impasse in the debate over reparations. Africa’s leaders are pressing harder than ever: the African Union has made 2026-2035 a decade of reparations . Former colonial powers offer words of regret, but carefully avoid any hint of material reparations.

The most prominent claims for reparations refer to vast historical wrongs perpetrated over centuries: the transatlantic slave trade, or colonial rule as a whole. Corresponding estimates of what is owed often run into trillions of dollars .

These claims carry great moral force. But they also raise questions that no court, and even fewer treasuries, can realistically begin to answer. Indeed, when the questions are so broad, there remains enormous ambiguity about who should pay whom, and on what legal basis.

Former colonial powers take advantage of this ambiguity to defer more substantive engagement. In March 2026, Britain argued at the United Nations that there is no duty to repair acts that were lawful when committed. In 2024, Portugal’s president said his country should take responsibility for its colonial past. His government replied that it had no process or programme for reparations.

Building on extensive prior research by the authors on specific colonial firms and forced labour in Mozambique and Angola, two new UNU-WIDER studies take a broader perspective and reflect on what can make financial reparations claims successful.

We find that the most tractable claims have been led by direct victims (“survivors”) of colonial injustices. Moreover, these claims refer to specific kinds of harms – ones that took place in living memory, breached legal standards applicable at the time, and can be quantified in terms of their duration, scope and (where possible) losses faced by victims.

Applying this logic, we argue that forced wage labour in Portuguese Africa represents a promising candidate for future reparations claims. Drawing on data from colonial archives, we estimate this system cost workers in Mozambique and Angola a cumulative total of around €1.2 billion, valued in contemporary prices.

A review of recent reparations cases

Our first study reviews the main colonial- and slavery-era reparations claims brought from sub-Saharan Africa since 2001. We group them by who has led the claim:

Survivors, such as the Kenyan Mau Mau veterans who sued the UK government. In 2013 Britain settled, paying £19.9 million to 5,228 victims of colonial-era abuse.

Indigenous groups, such as Herero and Nama descendants seeking redress from Germany for genocide in Namibia. Their lawsuit in the US was dismissed, and many community leaders rejected Germany’s 2021 offer of €1.1 billion in development funding , objecting to their exclusion from negotiations and to development aid being offered in place of reparations.

Read more: Germany’s genocide in Namibia: deal between the two governments falls short of delivering justice

States, such as African governments pressing former colonial powers for redress.

International organisations, such as the African Union’s continent-wide reparations agenda.

All four groups face obstacles, some shared and others specific to their claims. Politically, defendants must be willing to engage. Legally, claims must clear time limits and the question of what the law prohibited at the time. And, in most cases, someone must quantify the loss.

The record shows that survivor-led claims have proved by far the most tractable. While their obstacles are substantial, they are narrower.

We believe that the systematic use of forced labour in Portugal’s African colonies represents a strong prima facie case for survivor-led claims.

Read more: ‘The Night Trains’: a masterly study into southern Africa’s murderous migrant system

We take up this issue in detail in our second study , which seeks to quantify the scope and present-day value of the losses incurred by workers subject to this system during the 20th century.

Portuguese forced labour

From the late 19th century, Portuguese law imposed a duty on African men: to work in its colonies. Under what was known as the contrato system, colonial administrators helped recruit men in Angola and Mozambique for private employers such as plantations and mines. These men often worked alongside workers recruited on a voluntary basis, whose wages provide a benchmark for estimating the income lost under coercion. Pay was set far below what a free labour market would offer.

The system was formally abolished only in the early 1960s, but coercive recruitment did not disappear immediately. So, individuals and their families who were subject to this system remain alive today.

Our study pulls together data on the contrato system, estimating the number of people it encompassed and the income those subject to it lost between 1910 and 1974. To do so, we draw on firm wage records, labour statistics and fiscal accounts from colonial archives. We separate two questions: how many men were coerced, and what they would have earned in a labour market without coercion.

The statistics indicate that at its peak, the system forced up to one in five able-bodied men in the two colonies into wage labour. In some districts in certain periods the share was far higher. In Zambézia, in central Mozambique, over 90% of adult men were forcibly recruited by the late 1940s. Across both colonies, we estimate that the income taken from workers was equivalent to about 2.2 million years of earnings at voluntary wages.

Workers lost income in two connected ways: employers suppressed their wages, while the colonial state imposed taxes that helped compel them into wage work. Wage suppression accounts for about three quarters of the estimated loss, and its share grew in the final decades of colonial rule.

An earlier study of Sena Sugar Estates , once colonial Mozambique’s largest private employer, found coercion cut workers’ pay by about two-fifths. Research on Angola’s Diamang diamond mines provides complementary evidence: real earnings among workers recruited under contrato more than doubled between 1960 and 1965, following the formal abolition of forced labour in 1961.

Valued in 2023 euros, the total loss comes to about €1.2 billion. That is a fairly modest figure compared to trillion-dollar estimates for more encompassing historical harms.

But our estimate addresses the uncertainty that former colonial powers invoke: it is specific, transparent, and can be tested on the evidence.

A bill for specific harms

This figure is not the full bill for Portuguese colonialism. It leaves out, among other harms, violence, land seizures, unpaid public works and the earlier slave trade. It is best read as an estimate for one, well-documented harm. And while this focus may appear excessively narrow, our argument is that this specificity is exactly what can make such a case tractable, and move the debate towards reparatory justice.

Read more: Uganda-DRC reparations verdict raises questions about the price of justice

Indeed, a claim of this kind has identifiable victims, identifiable beneficiaries and a defensible number. Moreover, it does not rely on judging past acts by today’s law: forced labour, even where wages were paid, was already found to be in breach of international law while the contrato system continued to run. And some men conscripted in its final years during the 1960s are still alive, but now well past retirement age.

None of this replaces the broader political case for repair that the African Union and others are making. But apologies cost little. Claims grounded in solid evidence are harder to wave away. For surviving workers, the time to answer them is running out.

stories.title: Spotted on the D.C. Metro: Trump Staffer Accidentally Reveals Plan for Smithsonian Overhaul
stories.summary: The post Spotted on the D.C. Metro: Trump Staffer Accidentally Reveals Plan for Smithsonian Overhaul appeared first on ProPublica .

stories.body:
The man in the gray plaid suit on the Orange Line was working on his laptop in the crowded Metro train, revealing a draft plan for executive firings and sweeping changes at the National Museum of American History.

Since the Trump administration erupted this summer with criticism of the Smithsonian National Museum of American History for promoting “radical activist ideology” and precipitated the departure of Smithsonian secretary Lonnie Bunch, the White House’s next step on this front of the culture wars has been unclear.

Now the plan may have been revealed — inadvertently — in a crowded car on Washington, D.C.’s Metro transit system.

In the last week of October, as political Washington was focused on the coming midterm elections, a commuter on the Orange Line from the Northern Virginia suburbs was startled to see displayed, on the laptop of a man seated adjacent in a gray tartan suit, a document titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan.” The commuter snapped a few phone photos over the man’s shoulder and dispatched them to ProPublica.

Do You Have a Tip for ProPublica?

If you see something in public you think ProPublica should know about, there are a few ways you can reach us securely.

The 25-item list laid bare a comprehensive effort to completely transform the history museum, which employs several hundred people, is home to several million artifacts and draws close to 2 million visitors per year. If implemented in anything like the proposed form, it would represent an unprecedented assertion of White House control over the Smithsonian, which is structured to be independent.

Among the actions listed on the plan: firing the museum’s director, Anthea Hartig, and a dozen other top administrators and curators; announcing a new permanent exhibit called “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance” and an exhibit on “Great Families of American History”; and announcing a new “Colossus Statue” of George Washington for the museum’s entrance.

Other items on the list harkened back to a scathing 162-page critique of the museum released by the White House on July 4. That report was followed by back-to-back congressional hearings and a Trump executive order requiring signs to be erected outside the museum warning about the “ideological capture” on display there. While the pressure helped prompt Bunch’s departure as head of the Smithsonian, the warning signs have yet to go up, and it was unknown exactly what fixes the White House had in mind for the flaws that it so loudly decried.

Until now, perhaps. The plan displayed on the staffer’s laptop would issue new interpretative guidelines for exhibits, ending the museum’s reliance on a diversity style guide. It would review the Smithsonian’s strategy for traveling exhibitions, including halting one now underway, “The Bias Inside Us.” It would review the Smithsonian’s financial grants to “woke third parties” such as the American Alliance of Museums. And it would overhaul the museum’s online K-12 curriculum to “realign educational materials with patriotism, not ideology.” For instance, the website would drop the “Becoming US” module on immigration and launch a “Founders-focused curriculum titled something like Architects of Liberty: The Heroic Journey of America’s Founders OR Profiles in Liberty: Washington and America’s Heroic Men of Courage.”

The plan was apparently still a work in progress, given that the staffer had scribbled other proposals on a sheet of paper, also in plain view. They included “announce exciting cool exhibit on D-Day” and “no X rated exhibitions policy.” The latter item was a likely reference to something that drew a great deal of opprobrium in the July report and two congressional hearings that followed: a gay history exhibit that included a two-piece chrome and rubber crotch harness designed for sadomasochism.

At first, the identity of the staffer was undetermined, beyond a few clues including the fact that his initials were either B.S. or S.B., as displayed on his laptop. ProPublica reporters scoured White House staffing records to narrow down the list of candidates and took to the Orange Line to see if he would pop up again. Sure enough, there we saw the likeliest candidate, carrying the same style of brown leather satchel and same type of phone. He disembarked in Washington for the short walk to a White House employee checkpoint. It was Sam Bock, a 27-year-old associate policy adviser with the Domestic Policy Council, the White House office that produced the July report.

The White House did not respond to a query about the draft plan. Bock, who previously worked on the staff of Rep. Jim Jordan, the Ohio Republican elected last week as House Minority Leader, did not respond to messages. The Smithsonian, which bid farewell to Bunch at a board meeting last month, declined to comment.

The Smithsonian encompasses 20 museums beyond the American history one. It has a 17-member board that is led by the chief justice of the Supreme Court and comprises the U.S. vice president, three members of Congress from each party and nine private citizens nominated by other board members. But it relies on the federal government for the majority of its funding, receiving more than $1 billion per year, and its leadership is in a state of flux: Not only is it seeking to replace Bunch, but the board itself is riddled with vacancies as private citizen terms expire without replacements. Until President Donald Trump attempted to fire the director of the National Portrait Gallery last year, no president had tried to remove a Smithsonian executive. (The institution resisted, but the director, Kim Sajet, decided to leave anyway.)

As recounted by ProPublica in September , the American history museum has faced scrutiny over the years. Since its founding in 1964, it has struggled with the mission of telling the story of a vast and variegated nation; in 2001, an earlier round of criticisms prompted a blue-ribbon commission to produce a report urging the museum to offer a more unified approach to the national story, with fewer nods to political correctness. The Smithsonian underwent another identity crisis following the murder of George Floyd in Minneapolis in 2020, as Bunch and others led an institution-wide self-reckoning.

By the time of Trump’s return to office in 2025, there was no shortage of fodder for the new administration to seize on. The July report noted a recent exhibit on Ben Franklin that speculated about whether he had used enslaved members of his household as subjects of his experiments with electric shocks. And it chastised the museum for having trained staff using the “Museums as a Site for Social Action Toolkit,” a 200-plus-page tract on how to “truly transform the museum space,” which it says is linked “with white supremacy, hetero-patriarchy, abuse of labor, colonization, imperialist theft of art and artifacts, destruction or absencing of alternative ways of interpreting or representing art and artifacts, structural racism and other oppressions.”

The White House report emphasized that the museum should not whitewash blights on the nation’s history such as slavery and Jim Crow, but argued that it was failing to give visitors any sense of how it developed into the country that it is. “It should tell the whole story of a nation,” the report stated, “including the good and the bad, so Museum visitors can understand the development that led our nation to where it is today.”

The report was released with symbolic fanfare on the 250th anniversary of the nation’s founding. The administration’s announcement of its next move on this front may have less pop, given its soft rollout on the Orange Line.
