stories.imageAlt: A woman with glasses and highlighted hair wearing a black blazer over a pink patterned dress sits attentively in a pink armchair in a warmly lit room.
stories.body:
Immigrant women in abusive relationships have few places to turn for help. In the midst of an immigration crackdown in west Michigan, we traveled there to hear from women about how they calculate their safety. Some are afraid to leave the house.

About a dozen women chitchatted in Spanish between forkfuls of a tres leches cake. They spoke about their hopes and dreams — learning to drive, speaking English, visiting a son who had been deported. Some brought their young children, who scurried around them, circling the tables and tugging at their shirts, before the older kids nudged them into a nearby playroom, giving the women space to talk. The women were from Mexico and Guatemala, the Dominican Republic and El Salvador. Some settled here in west Michigan decades ago and had already become U.S. citizens or permanent residents. Others were more recent arrivals, with pending asylum cases. All of them said they had been abused by their current or former partners. And they had gathered at this informal support group, hosted by a local nonprofit, to talk.

I’m a ProPublica reporter in Detroit, and my colleague Melissa Sanchez is in Chicago. We each drove over 100 miles last summer to be in this room because we were working on a story. It published in mid-October, and it’s about how the immigration policies of President Donald Trump’s administration have made life more perilous for victims of domestic abuse . While reporting, we had heard about the pervasive presence of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in west Michigan, and we wanted to hear from immigrant women there who were living through domestic abuse. How did they weigh whether it was safer to stay with an abusive partner or to seek help from law enforcement, knowing they might be detained — and even deported?

That night, a young woman with a toddler told us that she called 911 about a year earlier, after her boyfriend slapped her when he was drunk. If he hit her today, she said, she wouldn’t dial that number again. With arrests by federal immigration officers constantly in the news, she said, the risk is too great.

None of the others in the room said they were currently living with an abusive partner. Those women were out there, the group’s facilitators told us. But they were too afraid to even leave their homes.

After the meeting, as empty paper plates were cleared from the tables, the facilitators told us about E. She was once a regular at the meetings, they said, but hadn’t been around in a while. They worried about her. We asked if E. might be open to talking with us and, after a few texts, we learned that she was — if we could be ready to talk in about 20 minutes.

We hurried back to our nearby lodgings, dialed E.’s number and put her on speakerphone. In Spanish, Melissa explained what we were reporting on, why it was so important to hear from somebody like her and the kinds of questions we wanted to ask. Then we began the interview.

E., who asked not to be fully identified, told us that she avoids going out unless it’s absolutely necessary. She’d heard harrowing stories about women at the immigration detention center in Michigan where other women we’d interviewed were locked up. As we described in our story, several had been arrested here in Kent County when local police responded to domestic violence calls. E. doesn’t want to end up in ICE custody herself or, worse, deported.

For the sake of her kids, E. said, she tolerates her husband’s abuse in silence.

When he tells her she’s “nobody here” and to “go back to your country,” she said she puts her head down. When he pulls her hair in bed and says she belongs to him, she said she pretends it’s a joke. When he asks for the money she makes from selling food at a local factory, she said she hands it over.

A filing in E.’s immigration case says her husband is a U.S. citizen who has been “verbally and financially abusive” and has threatened to take away the child they share. E. said that, except for the hair pulling, he isn’t physically abusive.

(Like the other women we interviewed, E. asked that ProPublica not interview her alleged abuser because she’s afraid he will retaliate against her, take away her children or call ICE. To report these women’s stories, we interviewed attorneys, advocates, family and others who interacted with them. When available, we also reviewed text messages, and records from law enforcement and immigration court.)

E. said her husband doesn’t overtly threaten her with calling ICE. But she said she found a hotline number for the agency written in his journal, alongside a description of his ideal woman: obedient and submissive.

That reminded us of what a local immigration attorney, Catherine Villanueva, had told us: “We have this idea that we’re deporting these really bad people,” she said. “What we’re doing is we’re empowering the bad people who are already here.”

We asked E. if she had ever called the police to report her husband’s abuse. Her answer came quickly: No. Her husband is frail. She worries police officers will look at both of them and decide that he’s the victim. “They won’t see me as the abused one,” she said. “If I called the police, the one who would wind up losing is me.”

When we reached out to federal officials for our story, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement that ICE is targeting the “worst of the worst.” The real story, she added, is the “American women whose lives have been taken by illegal alien criminals.” A spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that “we will never apologize for deporting illegal aliens, because that’s how we save lives.” As part of our reporting, we examined the backgrounds of the women we interviewed. Most had no criminal records we could find.

People in law enforcement and the prosecutor’s office in Kent County told us that they wanted everybody to feel safe reaching out to report crimes, regardless of their immigration status. Kent County Prosecutor Chris Becker said that he and a Spanish-speaking assistant prosecutor met with local advocates for immigrants who are victims of domestic violence “to try and lower that barrier, to make people understand that we see them as victims and want to serve them as victims.”

“But,” he added, “we can talk all we want, and still, I think it’s still difficult.”

Indeed, Angelica Ferrer, the victim witness coordinator in Becker’s office, said she used to be able to tell victims that if they came to court, “we’re not going to have ICE here.” She doesn’t say that to them anymore. “That is a choice that you have to make,” she said. “I can’t guarantee that you won’t be stopped on the way to court.”

Providing support for immigrants who are domestic abuse victims has long been extraordinarily difficult. But over five months of reporting, Melissa and I kept coming up against the same pervasive fear: In the current climate, nobody can really keep them safe.

Yet we heard from a lot of folks in Kent County who are trying to reach people like E., whether from positions in law enforcement, via social service agencies or as volunteers. Mary Sue Stegehuis, a retired teacher, is involved with a grassroots group called Hope for Neighbors. Even though she doesn’t know Spanish, she visits women in ICE custody, usually with a bilingual friend, and she stays in touch with them through a messaging app. She prints their stories — many involving domestic abuse — on homemade prayer cards, with an image of Mary, Joseph and Jesus migrating from Egypt on one side. Sharing the cards with others in the community, she told us, is meant to ensure that their stories don’t disappear, even if the women aren’t in the room to tell them.

We are still reporting on immigration and domestic abuse. If you have a tip or expertise, or you just want to share something you know, please get in touch. The Secretary-General of the PSOE Pedro Sanchez (left), and the leader of the PP Alberto Nuñez Feijoo (right), during a televised head-to-head debate (Shutterstock)

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez put a direct question to the leader of the conservative People’s Party (PP) and his principal rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo in Spain’s November 19 election debate. Did Feijóo regret his and PP’s No. 2 candidate Cayetana Álvarez de Toledo’s backing for Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu’s war on Iran?

Sánchez called the Iran war ‘disastrous,” invoking an equally disastrous precedent in Iraq more than 20 years ago. The question deliberately pointed to a PP government, led by the prime minister José María Aznar, that was one of the key champions of that misbegotten adventure.

Instead of responding directly, Feijóo took a convoluted detour by first claiming that Sanchez was the “only sitting MP who supported a war” by endorsing the Spanish parliament military intervention in Libya in 2011. But the intervention in Libya was backed by 336 members of the Spanish Congress, including those of Feijóo’s PP, several of whom are still in parliament.

Then Feijóo brought up unrelated matters, like the migration crisis in Ceuta earlier this year, before finally answering on the Iran war: “Of course I’m against it.” He then immediately added that Iran was “a dictatorship” and that Hamas and Hezbollah were “delighted” with Sánchez.

Sanchez missed an opportunity to press his rival on whether he would let the United States use the Spanish bases at Rota and Morón for another round of strikes on Iran should such a request come from Washington.

He had solid grounds for insisting on obtaining clear answers.

When the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February 2026, Álvarez de Toledo, Feijóo’s number two, expressed strong support for the operation and urged Spain and Europe to back it unequivocally. Former PP Prime Minister Aznar argued in March that a war to change Iran’s regime was justified. His neoconservative foundation, FAES (Fundación para el Análisis y los Estudios Sociales), still influential in parts of the PP, portrayed Sánchez’s opposition to the war as “ hypocritical and detrimental” to Spain.

Feijóo’s himself argued that Spain should preserve its relationship with Washington and put human rights ahead of international law in his criticism of Sánchez’s response to the war. Curiously, he and his party are considerably less insistent on human rights when it comes to close partners of the West, such as Israel or United Arab Emirates.

What Madrid would do in the case of another request for action by Washington depends not only on PP’s position but also on how much Feijóo would need the far-right party Vox after the November 29 election. The latest polls show that PP and Vox combined enjoy the support of almost half of the voters, while only around 40 percent favor the left bloc. The situation is in flux but the right and the far right could plausibly win an outright parliamentary majority.

Vox leader Santiago Abascal was straightforward in his support for Trump and Netanyahu. In April, he defended the U.S.–Israeli offensive as an exercise in pursuing national interests, while claiming, without citing any evidence, that the Iranian regime has killed 50,000 people and threatens the world with nuclear weapons.

The overlap between parts of PP and Vox has a history. Rafael Bardají, the Aznar adviser who pressed Spain to back the Iraq War, later joined Vox’s leadership team. In March 2026, he offered unconditional support for the U.S.- Israel war and attacked European leaders for failing to join it.

Bardají has spent years advocating for Israel and pressing for a harder line on Iran. He has served as the executive director of the Friends of Israel Initiative , a Madrid-based lobbying group that was launched in 2010 and led by Aznar, and that counts Iran ultra-hawks, such as John Bolton , among its co-founders. Bardaji also cultivated ties with neoconservative groups, like the UK-based Henry Jackson Society and the Washington DC-based Foundation for the Defense of Democracies.

A decision to allow the United States to use the Spanish bases in Rota and Morón or Spanish airspace to attack Iran would not be popular. In a March poll, 68 percent of Spaniards opposed the strikes and 53 percent backed the decision to deny the United States use of the bases for them.

A Feijóo government could reverse that position while continuing to say that it opposes war. A future U.S. request might concern refueling, transit, or logistical support. Madrid could authorize it while framing it as routine cooperation with an ally. This is the position taken by the center-right government in neighboring Portugal, which authorized the U.S. use of its airbase in the Azores islands while avoiding an open endorsement of the war.

The German Marshall Fund, a think-tank focusing on transatlantic relations, predicts that a PP-led government will take a more permissive stance on the use of the bases as part of an effort to repair relations with Washington. Feijóo’s own Atlanticist instincts—along with fear of Trump’s threats , the lingering influence of Aznar’s neoconservatism, and pressure from the ambitious hawks in his own party, such as Álvarez de Toledo and Madrid’s regional president Isabel Ayuso —would also likely push him in that direction. Vox, though more likely to focus its coalition bargaining on concerns like immigration and domestic policy, would reinforce these tendencies.

The choice would matter beyond Spain. Madrid has been one of the few European capitals willing to translate objections to U.S. and Israeli policy into concrete decisions: refusal to cooperate in any shape or form on the U.S. attack on Iran, an arms embargo on Israel, and the diplomatic recognition of Palestine. Reversing even one of those decisions would weaken Spain’s international standing and turn Madrid from a point of resistance to Trump into another European capital submissive to Washington and Tel Aviv.

stories.title: Paraguay’s Dark Sequel to It’s a Wonderful Life
stories.summary: A banking collapse exposed a deeper flaw in U.S. foreign policy: the tendency to confuse reliable partners with resilient democracies. The post Paraguay’s Dark Sequel to It’s a Wonderful Life appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
American actor James Stewart stands behind Donna Reed, gesturing with a handful of money while speaking to a group of townspeople in a still from the film, 'It's A Wonderful Life,' directed by Frank Capra, 1946. (RKO Pictures/Courtesy of Getty Images)

Frank Capra’s It’s a Wonderful Life is remembered for its faith in institutions, community, and public trust. Paraguay’s recent banking crisis offers a darker sequel. The collapse of Ueno Bank exposed not simply the failure of a financial institution but the consequences of a political system in which power, influence, and economic interests had become increasingly intertwined.

But the banking crisis did not create Paraguay’s underlying problem. It exposed something that had been developing for years: the growing capture of political and economic institutions by a powerful political machine centered on former president Horacio Cartes and his political protégé, Santiago Peña who became Paraguay’s president in 2023.

Paraguay’s banking crisis is not important merely because a major institution failed. It is important because it illustrates a recurring foreign-policy temptation: mistaking strategic or ideological alignment for evidence of democratic resilience.

The familiar bank-run scene in Capra’s film offers a useful point of comparison. Panic spreads, depositors demand their money, and George Bailey explains that the money is not sitting in a vault but invested throughout the community. The institution survives because people trust both the system and the people running it.

Paraguay’s crisis turned that premise on its head . The question many Paraguayans began asking was not merely where the money had gone. It was whether key institutions had come to serve a political elite rather than the public.

The problem was not simply that Washington missed warning signs. It was that many policymakers viewed Paraguay primarily through the lens of strategic and ideological alignment.

Paraguay’s standing in Washington rested on several factors. It remained one of Taiwan’s few diplomatic partners, maintained close relations with Israel , and increasingly aligned itself with influential conservative political movements in the United States. These attributes made Paraguay attractive as a geopolitical and ideological partner. But they also had an unintended consequence: governance concerns were increasingly overshadowed by other priorities. Evidence that would have prompted greater scrutiny elsewhere was often viewed through the assumption that a friendly government was also a healthy one.

The financial sector provided some of the clearest warning signs.

During Peña’s presidency, public funds increasingly flowed toward Ueno Bank, associated with Peña, and Banco Basa, long linked to Cartes. Government financial data showed an extraordinary concentration of public deposits and financial instruments in those institutions, while Paraguay’s social security system approved major purchases of Ueno bonds despite growing concerns about conflicts of interest. The developments prompted an obvious question: Why was the state directing so much public money toward institutions associated with the country’s most powerful political figures?

In October 2024, when a reporter asked Peña whether investments involving Ueno represented a conflict of interest, he angrily denounced the allegation as a “nefarious lie.” Nor were those concerns difficult to find in official U.S. assessments. The U.S. Department of State’s 2024 Investment Climate Statement warned that “unchecked corruption, impunity, and graft continue to hinder Paraguay’s economy.” Peña disputed the report, while senior Paraguayan officials dismissed it as inaccurate.

During this period, I observed a widening gap between how many Paraguayans understood their country’s trajectory and how it was often perceived in Washington. Conversations with journalists, civil-society leaders, businesspeople, and governance specialists frequently returned to concerns about the growing concentration of political and economic power around Cartes and his allies.

Among some policymakers and congressional observers in Washington, however, anti-corruption efforts were viewed less as responses to governance risks than as politically charged interventions . As a result, evidence of institutional deterioration was frequently filtered through ideological assumptions rather than evaluated on its own terms.

Yet Washington increasingly shifted attention away from governance concerns and toward geopolitical and ideological priorities. Sanctions were lifted , support for democracy and civil-society programs diminished, and anti-corruption efforts lost momentum. Whatever the rationale, the cumulative effect was to signal that institutional concerns were no longer paramount.

The collapse of Ueno finally exposed Paraguay’s crisis.

What appeared to be a banking scandal revealed a political system in which patronage networks, conflicts of interest, financial influence, and political authority had become deeply intertwined. The consequences were not abstract. Ueno’s failure left millions of customers unable to access their savings and disrupted payments and wages, while raising serious questions about the management of hundreds of millions of dollars in public deposits. For ordinary Paraguayans, the crisis was a deeply personal reminder of what happens when the institutions entrusted with protecting their financial security become entangled in political and economic power.

For years, Paraguayan cartoonists portrayed Peña as Cartes’ puppet. The caricature reflected a widely held perception that Peña’s political fortunes depended on the political machine Cartes built and continued to influence. When Cartes signaled support for Peña’s removal , the president’s political position unraveled with astonishing speed. Yet the larger lesson extends beyond any individual leader. The real issue was not the puppet but the system holding the strings.

Peña’s removal did not dismantle the machinery that had produced him. Pedro Alliana , who succeeded Peña as president, was one of Horacio Cartes’ closest political allies and had served as Peña’s vice president. Antonio Barrios , chosen to replace Alliana as vice president, had longstanding personal and political ties to Cartes. Although the transition altered the names at the top of the government, it did little to change perceptions that the same power structure remained firmly in place.

Paraguay matters not because it is unique but because it illustrates a temptation that recurs throughout American foreign policy. Policymakers naturally prefer partners who share their geopolitical priorities and ideological instincts. The danger comes when those affinities become substitutes for evaluating the strength of democratic institutions.

This is not just a Latin American story. Democracies rarely erode because leaders openly announce their intention to weaken institutions. More often, warning signs are rationalized away because the people benefiting from institutional decline are viewed as allies. Loyalty begins to outweigh accountability, and political convenience begins to outweigh democratic standards. By the time the consequences become impossible to ignore, many of the safeguards have already weakened.

Capra’s story endures because George Bailey reminds us that institutions are only as valuable as the communities they serve. Paraguay’s crisis tells the opposite story: what happens when institutions increasingly serve those who control them rather than the public that depends on them.

The dark sequel to It’s a Wonderful Life was never really about the bank. It was about the institutions behind it and the extent to which they had become vulnerable to political capture. Paraguay’s crisis should remind policymakers of a simple principle: strategic alignment and democratic resilience are not the same thing. When the former is allowed to obscure the latter, the consequences eventually become impossible to ignore.

stories.title: The Shenzhen Summit Supplants Yalta
stories.summary: The post The Shenzhen Summit Supplants Yalta appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
A world made safe for spheres of influence.

Nathan Gardels is the editor-in-chief of Noema Magazine. He is also the co-founder of and a senior adviser to the Berggruen Institute.

Pundits who dismissed the Shenzhen summit as a mere photo-op lacking substance missed the point. The significance of the conclave was precisely its enframing symbolism, showcasing a new world in which the rules-based order has been supplanted by spheres of influence accommodating each other.

The city of Shenzhen itself is a prism through which we can observe today’s power relations and the evolution of events over recent decades bringing us to this point.

Unplugged Computers in China’s Future Tech Hub

I first visited Shenzhen in 1986, arriving there by tram from Hong Kong and walking across the mainland border. There was barely any bustle, no crowds or traffic and a couple of tall buildings at the most. At our modest hotel, a squatting gardener was clipping the grass with a pair of scissors. The place still exuded the languorous vibe of the fishing village of 30,000 it had been not long before it was designated a “special economic zone” by Deng Xiaoping to attract foreign capital and technology.

On an inspection tour of sprouting industrial parks with then-former California governor Jerry Brown, our hosts proudly showed us what they called a tech hub. What then passed for “data centers” were cavernous, virtually empty warehouses with scores of desktop computers on worktables gathering dust — none were even plugged in.

What seemed embarrassing at the time turned out to be beyond impressive 40 years later. Shenzhen today is a literally glittering technopolis of 20 million people regarded as China’s “Silicon Valley” where Huawei, Tencent, DJI and BYD are all located. It is the center of gravity of China’s AI battle with the United States.

The invitation to visit had come some years earlier from Xi Zhongxun, then Party chief of Guangdong province (where Shenzhen is located) and the father of China’s current leader, Xi Jinping. The elder Xi had come to California in 1980 looking for investment in the special economic zone as a key platform of Deng’s policy of “reform and opening up” to the world. On that visit, he met Gov. Jerry Brown and toured the state, including stops at tech sites in the then-fledgling Silicon Valley (Apple and Intel were about it in those days) and Disneyland, where he gamely shook hands with Mickey Mouse.

Years later in 2012, when Brown was governor again for a second time, Xi Jinping, then-vice-president of China on his way to the top, visited California. The irony was not lost on either leader when the governor inquired whether China was interested in helping finance California’s bullet train, already in the works for nearly 20 years.

A Chinese delegation later met with the governor at the Peninsula Hotel in Beverly Hills to discuss possibilities, but the idea never panned out. Those who had once come cup in hand to the Golden State now offered financing terms too tough to abide. By 2026, China had built a 30,000-mile network of bullet trains spanning its vast country. California and the U.S. still have yet to build one.

On that 1986 trip to China, Brown and I also met at Zhongnanhai, the secluded leader’s compound in Beijing, with the ideology chief and youngest member of the ruling Communist Party Politburo at the time, Hu Qili. In a wide-ranging conversation that touched on topics from the “spiritual pollution” of Western influence to Tibetan Buddhism, Hu noted that the Chinese military had reduced its forces by one million soldiers. Many military installations, he said, were converting to commercial applications in light industry and heavy-truck production. Several military aircraft plants were now making refrigerators and motorcycles.

To this, Brown quipped, “If the army is making refrigerators, you must think the polar bear [what the Chinese called Russia] is hibernating.” Laughing, Hu simply replied that since Russia “couldn’t even consolidate control of Cambodia, it is only inviting great trouble to try anything with China.”

Opening then to America while hostile to an ebbing Soviet empire, Hu insisted that “China’s armed forces are sufficient to resist hegemonist efforts from the bear if they come.”

By the time I saw Hu again in 1988, Mikhail Gorbachev had come to power in the Kremlin, attracting some sympathy among reformers in China and inspiring a growing youth movement with his ideas of perestroika and glasnost. Enough of a thaw was in the works that Hu asked me to convey “fraternal greetings” to Aleksandr Yakovlev, then the Soviet party’s main reformist thinker, on my next stop in Moscow. Read Noema in print.

“The one key power left out of the 1945 Yalta talks that shaped the international order in the dying days of World War II is now setting the agenda for what comes next.”

The Tiananmen Turn

It was in that atmosphere that Gorbachev visited Beijing in May 1989 and met with Premier Zhao Ziyang as tensions with the authorities were mounting on Tiananmen Square. In the wake of the student massacre that June, the liberal-leaning Zhao was purged for revealing “state secrets” to Gorbachev by telling him that Deng, who would order the repression, remained the power behind the throne even though he had formally retired. Hu was also purged.

This was a “ludicrous accusation,” Gorbachev told me later. The real issue, as he saw it, was his advice that the student occupation should be defused politically through negotiation, not force. “I was confident a political solution could be found. I was wrong, unfortunately,” the last Soviet leader lamented.

Deng had drawn the line on Party control that Gorbachev was erasing in Moscow. Deng’s open palm on the economy clenched into an iron fist on political reform. Ever since, Gorbachev’s “new thinking” has been vilified in Beijing as a recipe for the collapse of the Party-state, and something to be avoided at all costs.

A World Safe For Spheres Of Influence

When Vladimir Putin emerged in the tumultuous years after the Soviet collapse, China’s sympathy with a more amenable Russia returned. As the post-Cold War years wore on, the “hegemonist threat” for China shifted to America, even as it prospered from the relationship.

In the end, China’s leaders came to strategically favor a trusted autocrat ruthlessly obsessed with dominating his own neighborhood over a meddling America endlessly endeavoring, in their minds, to subvert China’s governing system and keep the nation down. Party ideologues, Xi above all, are convinced that the American political class, implicitly if not explicitly, concurs with Bill Clinton’s remark when he was president that China was on “the wrong side of history.” Like many others in those days, Clinton wrongly presumed trade winds would blow open the society.

With a militarily mighty but economically feeble and dependent Russia at its side, China’s leaders have grown more confident in their capacity to contain America in a world made safe for spheres of influence.

The few words spoken for public consumption at the Shenzhen summit about zones of “civilizational values” and the primacy of state sovereignty over international law were code for the long-standing views of Xi and Putin, which the American president has now openly embraced.

Tech Trips The Thucydides Trap

At the first meeting of the Berggruen Institute’s 21st Century Council with Xi Jinping in 2013, the Party leader boasted that “we have never been closer to realizing the dream of Chinese rejuvenation” after the long climb back from colonial humiliation — invoking that history as if it were yesterday.

As Xi sees it, far from being on the wrong side of history, only the firm hand of the Communist Party could have brought the Middle Kingdom to where it is today and can take it where it must go tomorrow.

In 2015, then Premier Li Keqiang launched a “Made in China 2025” campaign with the goal of conquering the latest technologies from electric vehicles and batteries to artificial intelligence within a decade. Xi sees this conquest as rocket fuel for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, which he is determined to ensure does not fall behind the West and invite domination by outside forces, as it did during the Ming and Qing dynasties of the late 19th Century.

Strategists in Washington across the partisan landscape see China’s unrelenting resolve to reach its goals as an existential threat to America’s technological supremacy, and all that implies in terms of military might and geopolitical sway.

At our 2013 meeting, Xi pointedly raised an historical reference to “the Thucydides Trap,” whereby a rising power inevitably runs into conflict with an established power, only to say China would seek to avoid it. By now, though, it is clear that of all the contested issues between the U.S. and China, technology is most likely to trip the trap. The Nvidia episode is but one skirmish in a larger battle.

Shenzhen Supplants Yalta

If I were to have a conversation with the ideology chief on the Politburo today, as I had with Hu decades ago, here is what I would imagine him saying: “We have demonstrated we can go head-to-head with America on AI and technology. Today our military is reinvigorated. We have the largest navy in the world and are scaling up our nuclear arsenal toward parity with the U.S. and Russia. To be sure, America remains a formidable foe with the legacy of hegemonist ambitions. But let’s be serious. It is crumbling within. Its aging systems are plagued by outages. It can’t even build one bullet train.”

For Xi, hosting both leaders of the other great powers in Shenzhen, where China’s tech prowess is on full display, is the ultimate icing on the cake of rejuvenation. The one key power left out of the 1945 Yalta talks that shaped the international order in the dying days of World War II is now setting the agenda for what comes next.

stories.title: Russia, India, and Saudi Arabia Are Stalling a Key U.N. Climate Report
stories.summary: Experts are warning that political attacks on a critical scientific report could undermine the basis for future U.N. climate negotiations. Read more on E360 →
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
This article was originally published by Inside Climate News and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

A coal mine in Jharkhand, India. Vishal Kumar Singh / AFP via Getty Images via Inside Climate News

Experts are warning that political attacks on a critical scientific report could undermine the basis for future U.N. climate negotiations.

The science that guides negotiators and policymakers at the United Nations’ COP31 climate change conference is “under a serious and highly politicized attack,” said Laurence Tubiana, a veteran French climate diplomat and one of the architects of the 2015 Paris climate agreement.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, established in 1988 to inform international climate negotiations, regularly assesses thousands of studies on rising temperatures, sea level rise, melting ice, and strategies for adapting to the increasingly intense impacts of global warming.

But three countries — Russia and Saudi Arabia, both major fossil fuel producers, and India, which accounts for an estimated 14 percent of global coal consumption — are blocking progress on future reports, according to scientists on the panel and independent observers.

Those countries “are doing everything they can to slow the process,” Tubiana said. They are becoming less discreet about their efforts, she said, as they increasingly view their economies as threatened by a conditional agreement to transition away from coal, oil, and gas reached during COP28, the 2023 Conference of the Parties in Dubai.

The science panel’s current impasse is especially troubling, “because we know climate problems are accelerating, and we need a lot of data and communication to understand what’s happening at this COP,” said Mary Robinson, former president of Ireland and former United Nations special envoy on climate change.

Robinson said this isn’t the first time countries have tried to obstruct science. Recent examples include attacks seeking to undermine a recent United Nations Environment Programme report on “overshoot,” which concludes that there is no way to avoid passing the 1.5 degree C warming target in the Paris Agreement.

Fossil fuels account for an estimated 80 percent to 90 percent of planet-heating carbon dioxide emissions, according to the IPCC’s 2023 assessment .

The international climate science panel relies on voluntary donations from member countries to fund its work, including periodic assessments, some of which inform steps required under the Paris Agreement. The panel has yet to set a budget for next year, potentially delaying a scientific report needed ahead of next year’s U.N. climate conference.

“Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the oil and gas sector has become much more aggressive,” Tubiana said. “I think this is partly because it sees its dominance over energy starting to erode.”

Oil and gas companies are losing ground in transport as electric-vehicle adoption in Asia surges faster than expected, she said, adding that reports from the International Energy Agency show demand for fossil fuels is set to slow.

“Investors hear the message that the decline is coming, and those governments have pushed back,” she said.

The 2023 IPCC report concluded that existing and planned fossil fuel infrastructure would push global warming beyond the Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming as close as possible to 1.5 degrees C above the preindustrial average.

Tubiana said a growing number of countries view the transition away from fossil fuels as a path to greater energy independence and security, while those opposed to the shift are becoming “more angry and vocal.”

“The danger,” she said, “is that they take other countries along with them that aren’t necessarily committed to that position.”

The latest draft of the conference’s decision document highlights the assessments’ importance to the negotiations. Some countries also want to include language that could help break the science panel’s deadlock, but the same countries stalling the IPCC are resisting that effort.

In particular, the climate, environment, and energy ministers participating in the current round of talks could help the IPCC get over the political hurdles it faces, said Bill Hare, CEO of Climate Analytics, an international climate science and policy institute.

Hare said the countries participating in the U.N. talks should advocate for continued support for the IPCC. If the panel can’t deliver the needed climate science “because of political obstacles created by a small number of countries, it would be a historic setback for the connection between science and the international climate process.”

Robinson said some of the world’s least developed countries and small island states “desperately need” the international panel’s reports because they can’t do their own climate assessments.

“We need the authoritative, legitimate IPCC science, which has guided us from the beginning in this whole climate process,” she said. “It’s just a sign of the difficult times we’re in that we have to fight for it. I can hardly believe it.”

— Bob Berwyn , Inside Climate News

stories.title: What China’s Gene-Editing Deaths Reveal About Its Biotech Industry
stories.summary: The post What China’s Gene-Editing Deaths Reveal About Its Biotech Industry appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Regulation alone won’t fix the conditions that have earned China the reputation of the “Wild East.”

Jane Qiu is an independent science writer in Beijing.

BEIJING — In March 2023, four-year-old Mei in Shanghai was diagnosed with a rare genetic mutation linked to developmental delay and autism-like traits. Although her condition was mild and she improved with therapy and special education, her parents remained worried about her future. Hopeful for a cure, they paid Qiu Zilong, a renowned neuroscientist at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and his team $860,000 to develop a customized gene therapy. The treatment, which used adeno-associated viruses to deliver gene editors to the brain, had been approved by Xinhua Hospital, a leading hospital for rare diseases.

On March 24, 2025, trillions of viral particles carrying gene editors were injected into Mei’s spinal cord. She soon developed a fever and kidney failure and died within days. A year later, Qiu’s team published its preclinical findings in Nature, which Chinese media hailed as “a world-class breakthrough.” Mei’s death and her family’s financial support were not mentioned.

Deaths in clinical trials are not unusual. What is shocking are the regulatory lapses revealed by an investigation published this July in Science and subsequently corroborated by a separate investigation conducted by the Shanghai municipal government, which released its findings last week. The treatment’s consent form, for instance, didn’t warn of the possibility of death. The hospital had approved treatment before toxicology findings showing liver and kidney damage in monkeys that received similar treatments. And, among other crucial omissions, the researchers failed to disclose Mei’s death.

Apparently, this was not an isolated incident. Several researchers told me that Chinese hospitals commonly fail to disclose adverse events. On Aug. 5, STAT reported another death in a gene-editing trial led by Shanghai-based HuidaGene, an incident that had remained undisclosed for about 15 months. (The Chinese team published their findings , including the fatal case, in Cell on Oct. 26.) A founder of a rare-disease organization in China told me, on condition of anonymity for fear of political repercussions, that she had encountered other trials for genetic disorders in which deaths had gone unreported. Recent revelations of undisclosed deaths in clinical trials conducted in China have prompted warnings against the use of Chinese data in U.S. drug development.

As someone who has reported on China’s ethical governance for two decades, this all feels like déjà vu. Since modern bioethics was introduced to China in the late 1980s, its history has been punctuated by one scandal after another — often fueled by hype surrounding emerging technologies — that have earned the country a reputation as biotechnology’s “Wild East.”

Back in 2006, patients flocked to China to receive unproven stem-cell therapies . When immunotherapies came into vogue a decade later, bogus advertisements for unproven interventions proliferated online until the health ministry stepped in after the high-profile death of 21-year-old student Wei Zexi. Two years later, biophysicist He Jiankui shocked the world by announcing the birth of the first genetically modified babies created using CRISPR technology.

The response in China to Mei’s death has been divided. Some netizens portray Qiu as a reckless scientist willing to gamble with patients’ lives. Others, including longtime acquaintances, describe him as a diligent scientist committed to helping patients. In some respects, Qiu represents the antithesis of He. After the CRISPR-babies scandal, Qiu openly condemned He’s reckless behavior — only to become embroiled in a comparable scandal himself six years later.

It might be tempting to blame such scandals on individual failings. The deeper questions are: What systemic factors shaped their behavior? What does the incident reveal about China’s Achilles heel in biotechnology—and about the broader culture of international science in which it is embedded? And what can the lessons teach clinical research worldwide?

Fatal Flaw

It would be unfair to suggest that China hasn’t tried to strengthen its ethical governance. The CRISPR-babies scandal prompted deep soul-searching among Chinese scholars and government officials. Since then, President Xi Jinping reportedly championed an “ethics first” approach, contrasting the “science first” mindset often seen in Chinese research. New measures have included incorporating ethics provisions in China’s first Civil Law Code, creating a national ethics committee , and enacting new ethics-review guidelines for clinical research.

But powerful forces are also pushing in the opposite direction. In 2016, China launched Healthy China 2030, making rapid application of emerging medical technologies in clinical practice a priority — not only to address unmet medical needs but to boost national competitiveness. Reforms created a new pathway to translate basic research into clinical applications for cutting-edge technologies overseen by the health ministry, alongside the conventional drug-approval route regulated by the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA), China’s equivalent of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). This became widely known as the dual-track regulatory system.

“Since modern bioethics was introduced to China in the late 1980s, its history has been punctuated by one scandal after another — often fueled by hype surrounding emerging technologies.”

Under the technology track, clinical trials are often initiated by university researchers working with hospital clinicians rather than companies. Such investigator-initiated trials (IITs) exist worldwide. Until new regulations took effect this May, Chinese IITs were distinctive in that they could proceed with hospital approvals without the national regulatory oversight required for conventional drug trials. Compared with the NMPA route, the faster pathway allowed researchers to assess promising technologies in humans more quickly and at lower costs and help attract investment.

The result was a boom in IITs. By one estimate , more than 40,000 had been registered by April 2026, involving hundreds of thousands of participants and accounting for much of China’s translational research aimed at applying basic research to clinical practice.

China’s IIT model attracted worldwide attention. Kiran Musunuru, an expert on gene therapy at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, told me that “there is a widespread perception” that Chinese-style IITs offer a way to conduct first-in-human trials quickly and inexpensively. U.S. companies are increasingly interested in conducting IITs in China. Some U.S. researchers have even argued that the U.S should adopt elements of China’s model to accelerate drug discovery and enhance its competitiveness.

Critics, however, point to a fatal flaw: quality control. Driven by the pursuit of high-impact papers— whether for career advancement or hospital rankings — researchers rushed into first-in-human trials of emerging technologies. Hospitals are overwhelmed by proposals involving technologies with varying levels of risk. Researchers told me that as many as two dozen applications can be assessed in a single afternoon. In many cases, the process has become “a rubber-stamping exercise,” explained Zhu Wei, a bioethicist at the Shanghai Clinical Research Center.

A recent analysis of Chinese stem-cell IITs found that although a small fraction helped accelerate the application of basic research to clinical practice, most were repetitive, lacked innovation and wasted resources. Musunuru — who led the landmark development of a personalized gene-editing trial for Baby KJ, an infant with a rare life-threatening deficiency of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 that can cause dangerous ammonia buildup in the blood — warns that allowing individual hospitals to approve first-in-human trials of emerging technologies is particularly dangerous, because few researchers have sufficient experience to assess their risks. They would be “operating blind,” he told me, leaving the outcome dependent on “their appetite for risk.” That appetite can be amplified by institutional conflicts of interest. Successful trials of emerging technologies can bring researchers and hospitals fame, career advancement, high rankings and resources. Jing-Bao Nie, a bioethicist at the University of Otago in Dunedin, New Zealand, told me that these incentives can undermine institutional judgment and jeopardize patient safety. In Mei’s case, he noted, the lure of a “world-class breakthrough” may have overwhelmed necessary caution. Political interference, which is common in China, is another way the appetite for risk may outweigh caution. Chinese researchers told me that senior hospital leaders often chair the committees that review trial applications. When they seek to push through major projects led by prominent scientists, other committee members may feel unable to object. Read Noema in print. A central regulator is more insulated from such pressures and can also draw on a far broader pool of expertise. As Musumuru notes, the FDA has an army of experienced reviewers who have assessed successful and failed trials, as well as those involving serious adverse effects. Its decisions are therefore informed by “the widest possible body of knowledge,” he told me. “That’s very reassuring.” Oversight Deficiencies Zhai Xiaomei, a bioethicist at the Peking Union Medical College and a member of the national science and technology ethics committee, was not wrong when she told New Beijing News that the problems exposed by Mei’s tragedy had improved since China’s State Council Order No. 818, which established a new regulatory framework for clinical research and commercial application of cutting-edge biomedical technologies, took effect this May. Under the new rules, only top-tier hospitals can undertake IITs. Trials involving emerging technologies like gene and cell therapy, brain-machine interfaces, transplantation and microbial therapies must undergo further review by the health ministry after hospital approval. Adverse effects must be reported within five working days. Violations can result in fines, suspension or permanent ban on clinical research, loss of licenses and even criminal charges. The scientific community in China and abroad welcomes the new rules. But a researcher working closely with the ministry, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to potential career repercussions, told me that it lacks sufficient staff with the necessary technical expertise to review the large volume of applications. Consequently, the researcher added, the reviews rely heavily on experts from universities and hospitals, with only a handful assessing each case. By contrast, Musunuru told me that the U.S. FDA employs numerous in-house reviewers, many with decades of experience, and dozens pore over each submission. If translating emerging technologies into clinical practice remains a national priority, he argues, China must make sustained investments in regulatory expertise to ensure trial safety and quality. “If translating emerging technologies into clinical practice remains a national priority, China must make sustained investments in regulatory expertise to ensure trial safety and quality.” More troublingly, Order 818 lacks mechanisms to monitor what happens locally and identify violations. It includes neither an inspection process — a crucial component of regulatory oversight in countries such as the U.S. and UK — nor a whistleblowing platform for reporting adverse effects and deaths. Such mechanisms are particularly important in countries where transparency is limited, and the press is not free. Without them, violations may go unnoticed and the penalties risk becoming little more than empty threats. Researchers, like bioethicist Ma Yonghui of Xiamen University, also worry that regulatory exemptions could create loopholes. Military hospitals, for instance, fall outside health ministry rules. The two dozen or so free trade zones across China, particularly in Bo’ao on the tropical island of Hainan, may enjoy special regulatory treatment, potentially attracting foreign researchers and companies seeking to conduct ethically contentious trials they could not undertake in their own countries. There are ample precedents of scientists exploiting countries with weak ethics governance as sites for risky research. In October 2018, one month before the CRISPR-babies scandal, He and John Zhang, founder and medical director of the New Hope Fertility Center in New York City, met Hainan’s vice governor to discuss establishing a clinic in Bo’ao to offer experimental procedures, including heritable genome editing. Zhang had already attracted international attention in 2016 for helping produce in Mexico the world’s first “three-parent baby” to prevent the transmission of mitochondrial DNA mutations from the mother. The procedure involved replacing faulty mitochondria with healthy ones from a female donor during in vitro fertilization, a procedure that was — and still is — illegal in the U.S. Hype & Hope While Mei’s death has prompted renewed soul-searching over China’s ethical failings, it would be a mistake to see it simply as a scientific scandal that can be fixed with new regulations, Nie told me. The case offers a window into people’s relationship with biotechnology in China as well as their hopes and expectations — shaped not only by scientists but by society at large. Over the past decade, rare-disease advocacy organizations have grown rapidly in China, helping improve patient care, pressing for government support and driving research through collecting genetic data, studying disease progression and funding clinical trials. Su Yeyang, an independent anthropologist in Langfang in Hebei province who works with rare-disease communities, told me this has given families a sense of agency. With limited social support and a market-driven drug-discovery model that has failed rare-disease communities worldwide, they are doing whatever they can “to help themselves, their children and their community,” she said. With gene therapy, the “magic cure” long hoped for by many rare-disease patients seems within reach. In one high-profile case, a fledgling company approached Xu Wei, a high-school graduate in his 30s in Kunming, in China’s southern province of Yunnan, to develop a gene therapy for his son. The boy had Menkes syndrome, a rare genetic disorder that impairs copper absorption and causes developmental delays and premature death. The company, with no track record in neurodevelopmental diseases, claimed to have developed the treatment in less than a year. In 2022, the 3-year-old received it at a private hospital in a trial that, based on publicly available accounts, appeared not to include biomarker or behavioral assessments of efficacy. Chinese media reported enthusiastically on anecdotal claims of improvements while downplaying the risks of undertaking such experimental therapies. A patient advocacy leader told me such cases are not uncommon in China, where at least 20 million people are living with rare diseases. They offer hope, whether grounded in evidence or not, and can encourage others to follow. “We try to explain to families that pouring millions into a trial is no guarantee of success” and could even backfire, she says. Even well-educated parents, like Mei’s, may underestimate the complexity of clinical research and overestimate what experimental therapies can achieve. It’s unclear whether Qiu, who was fired by the university last week and barred from participating in scientific research for five years following the government investigation , helped foster such expectations. He has not publicly given his account. But his book, “ The Autism Enlightenment ,” published this April, was revealing. It recounted how, in 2010, he told the mother of a child with Rett syndrome — a rare, genetic neurodevelopmental disorder leading to severe cognitive and physical impairments — that a cure would likely emerge in three to five years. It did not discuss fatal risks often associated with first-in-human trials. It did not mention Jessie Gelsinger, who had a mild form of ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, a condition that can lead to abnormally high levels of ammonia in the blood and died in 1999 from a preventable complication of an experimental gene therapy. “While Mei’s death has prompted renewed soul-searching over China’s ethical failings, it would be a mistake to see it simply as a scientific scandal that can be fixed with new regulations.” Gelsinger was the first person publicly identified as having died in a gene therapy clinical trial, which undermined public trust in the field and set back its progress for decades. Nor did the book draw caution from the death in 2024 of a girl with Rett syndrome in the first brain-directed gene therapy for the condition. In both cases, scientists used the same type of virus as Qiu did. In a society where disability and genetic disease remain stigmatized, and families receive limited support, Mei’s parents placed their hopes in Qiu and gene editing. Like the couple who turned to He Jiankui to protect their children from HIV and the associated discrimination by editing their embryos, they sought a technological solution to social problems. As the Illness Challenge Foundation, a Beijing-based rare-disease advocacy organization, put it after Mei’s death , “responsible innovation should not entice patients to stake their lives in the name of hope.” China’s Gelsinger Moment? Gelsinger’s death in 1999 was a game changer. It’s widely regarded as a cautionary tale of how a toxic combination of scientific hype and insufficient safeguards can jeopardize patient safety. It triggered institutional reforms and significant changes in research culture in the U.S. that were aimed at rebuilding public and regulatory trust. Mei’s death could be China’s Gelsinger moment. It has exposed regulatory failings, a scientific ethos that encourages hype and recklessness, and deeper societal problems surrounding disability and genetic disease. None is unique to China, but they are particularly acute in a country facing a distinctive combination of political and developmental challenges. At the heart of the incident lies the “moral arbitrage” of experimental therapies, a recurrent theme in biotechnological innovation worldwide. On one hand, patients want access to cutting-edge, unproven treatments when they see them as their only hope. On the other hand, such treatments carry risks, which often accompany medical breakthroughs. Navigating the contours between hope and risk requires more than scientific evidence and regulatory rules, Su told me. It demands critical reflection on the culture of international science that places a premium on competition, sensational research, and being first at any cost. It also calls for broader societal dialogues about the diverse notions of human flourishing, the stigmatization of disabilities, and the need for greater support for people living with rare diseases. If China can learn from the failures and undertake the regulatory, scientific and social reforms needed to address its biotech governance failures — and if the rest of the world can look beyond the country’s small number of success stories out of a hidden ocean of low-quality and potentially harmful clinical trials — Mei’s death will not have been in vain. Delegation of 50 to accompany minister, with trip criticised after universities were warned about Chinese interference

The education secretary, Lucy Powell, is travelling to Beijing this week to promote UK education, weeks after MI5 issued a rare public warning to universities about Chinese interference in UK academia.

A 50-strong UK delegation, including 18 university leaders, will accompany the minister when she attends the first UK-China education summit in nine years, aimed at opening up new opportunities for universities, colleges and education businesses.

The visit prompted criticism, as it comes two months after UK universities were warned by MI5 that China’s intelligence services were using a front company to pay for research by UK academics and steal secrets from hi-tech projects.

One critic described Powell’s visit, which begins on Tuesday, as “mind-blowingly shortsighted”, while the Conservatives said the education secretary’s priorities were “all wrong”.

Discussions in China are expected to cover higher education, technical and vocational education, schools, English language teaching, digital education and education technology, the Department for Education (DfE) said

“The freedom and independence of our academic institutions is sacrosanct,” a DfE spokesperson said. “We will not accept collaborations which compromise our national security or attempt to benefit covertly from research done in partnership with UK universities.”

Successive British governments have welcomed Chinese investment and encouraged academic cooperation between the two countries. About 150,000 Chinese students currently study at UK universities, contributing £7bn to the UK economy every year. Concerns have been growing in recent years, however, about the potential risks of such close collaboration.

On 30 September, MI5 warned vice-chancellors that a Chinese state-owned conglomerate called the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI) had funded 100 or more academics in return for access to research which found its way back to China’s intelligence service.

The claim was denied by the Chinese embassy. Before that there was outcry when it emerged Sheffield Hallam University had complied with a demand from Beijing to halt research about human rights abuses in China .

Condemning the trip to China, the shadow education secretary, Laura Trott, said Powell’s priorities were all wrong. “Instead of seeking closer ties to China, Powell should clamp down on CCP [Chinese Communist party] attempts to influence our own universities & its treatment of those who criticise it,” she posted on X.

Luke de Pulford, the executive director of the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China, wrote on X: “Mind-blowingly shortsighted in policy terms.”

“What might seem to the uninitiated like an economic opportunity, or short-term hope to plug a gap in finances may actually be the government signing UK high education’s death warrant.

“If the balance tips too far towards dependence; if Beijing gets enough leverage, these institutions will cease to operate freely, and continue to leak IP and sensitive research to an adversary.”

after newsletter promotion

Sam Dunning, the director of UK-China Transparency, said the UK was in unprecedented territory. “British universities have never been so financially dependent on foreign students as they are today on Chinese students,” he said.

“Nor have there ever been more foreign nationals from any one country than British nationals studying Stem at an elite level in our top institutions, as is the case with China today.

“We are in unprecedented territory and on perilous terrain. The public interest demands careful, long-term thinking about these issues, and not continued short-termism.”

The summit forms part of government plans to grow education exports to £40bn a year by 2030. “British education is one of our country’s greatest strengths,” said Powell. “Expanding that internationally is a massive opportunity for our economy and wider society.

“Education builds lasting relationships and creates opportunities, but it also gives us the relationships and channels we need to have open and honest conversations. That is why we are putting education at the heart of clear-eyed engagement with China, using Britain’s world-class reputation to support growth, strengthen our global standing and stand up for what matters to Britain.”

stories.title: Burnham does not view Wales as an equal nation, claims first minister
stories.summary: The first minister asks for urgent meeting after Andy Burnham rejected calls for more powers in Cardiff.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Andy Burnham says he's "not persuaded" by the case for more powers

Published 23 November 2026

The first minister says he wants an urgent meeting with the prime minister after Andy Burnham rejected calls to give more powers to the Welsh government.

Rhun ap Iorwerth said he was "deeply disappointed" and that Burnham "does not view Wales as an equal nation".

Meanwhile, Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates urged Burnham to "negotiate around a table" with ap Iorwerth.

In a letter to ap Iorwerth last week, the prime minister said he was "not persuaded" by the case to devolve policing and justice , the Crown Estate and rail infrastructure to Wales.

Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock said the UK government believed "devolution must be about more than transferring powers from one government to another".

Trade union body TUC Cymru said it was disappointing calls for further devolution had been "dismissed without any discussion".

In a written statement to Senedd members, the first minister said: "The refusal to even explore the devolution of the crown estate, justice and policing, and rail infrastructure proves that the prime minister does not view Wales as an equal nation.

"The case in favour of Wales having control over these areas of responsibility – just like Scotland – is compelling. Several commissions have argued for the devolution of justice and policing, yet the UK government seemingly prefers to put unionist ideology before hard evidence.

"This government is not interested in more powers for power's sake. The current settlement is unfair, unjust and unsustainable."

Rhun ap Iorwerth is Plaid Cymru leader and first minister of Wales

In a letter to the prime minister, ap Iorwerth asked the prime minister to reconsider the work of previous reports on the issue.

He said he would "welcome an urgent meeting with you to discuss the evidence and agree a substantive way forward".

Meanwhile, Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates called on the Welsh and UK governments to continue talks on the devolution of powers.

He called for "greater detail" on why further devolution of policing was not happening, and said he will be meeting with Burnham himself.

Welsh Labour has not dropped calls for the devolution of justice, the Crown Estate and rail investment.

"You negotiate around a table," he said. "And you don't walk away when work needs to continue. Devolution is a process, not an event and Welsh Labour's position remains clear that we support further devolution to and within Wales."

Skates continued: "Devolution of employment support is vital in getting to grips with the crisis of youth unemployment. The devolution of innovation funding will help strengthen the economy.

"Devolution of youth justice will lead to better integration of youth services and social services and the justice system.

"We need action as fast as possible in bringing these powers to Wales and in ensuring they go to the right people and places.

"On policing, progress is being made, but I want greater detail over why full devolution is not happening as part of the current reforms."

Meanwhile, TUC Cymru's general secretary, Laura Doel, said: "Our focus is on securing the powers and resources needed to improve outcomes for working people. That must include fair funding for Wales.

"These are the long-established views of TUC Cymru and it's disappointing that our calls have been dismissed without any discussion.

"We ask that the UK government does more to respect and engage with the democratic institutions in Wales and listens to the voice of Welsh workers, rather than closing down proposals for further devolution before they have been properly considered."

Kinnock said: "The prime minister's offer reflects our view that devolution must be about more than transferring powers from one government to another and that he instead wants each government to consider, alongside local authority partners, how we can empower Welsh regions to use both reserved and devolved powers to drive economic growth.

"What matters is what works."

stories.title: Jensen Huang’s reported affair was ‘most expensive sex since Helen of Troy’, US senator says

John Kennedy looks to Trump leaders as he asks how China evidently bypassed export controls for Nvidia’s top AI chips

Invoking Greek mythology, the US senator John Kennedy has characterized former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang ’s reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy as “the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy”.

The Louisiana Republican’s allusion to the legendary figure whose desirability was such that it caused the mythic Trojan war came during an interview on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday. Host Kristen Welker asked Kennedy, known for his colloquialisms, if US national security was put at risk by Huang’s affair, given the position his company’s chips have occupied at the forefront of the artificial intelligence boom.

Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO on 12 November after allegations surfaced of extramarital relationships with the suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang and two Nvidia employees.

Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, had been executive director of Megaspeed International. Megaspeed facilitated about $12bn in chip sales, in violation of export controls in the US, by which the Trump administration has prohibited the selling of advanced AI chips to China.

On Sunday’s edition of CNN’s State of the Union , the Trump administration’s national intelligence director, Jay Clayton, said he suspected China was able to obtain Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips.

He also said on Fox News Sunday: “There are chips that have ended up in places that they should not.”

Kennedy said he was “less interested in … what [Huang] did” than in asking the Trump administration’s commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick , and its treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, about how China was evidently able to circumvent US “export controls”.

“Mr Huang … did what he did. I hope he had a good time. It was the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy,” Kennedy said.

Lutnick has faced scrutiny over allegedly ignoring warnings that Megaspeed was smuggling chips to China. Other administration leaders, including Bessent, wanted to put Megaspeed on a trade blacklist – but the commerce department stalled enforcement of it.

Kennedy said he could only conclude commerce department leaders were either “so incompetent you wouldn’t put them in charge of a food truck” – or “they knowingly allowed this to happen”.

He said he wanted to get Bessent and Lutnick under oath in front of a Senate committee to “answer some hard questions”.

“And if Secretary Lutnick is giving our chips away, he needs to stop it, in my opinion,” Kennedy said.

Bessent said on Sunday’s edition of CBS News’s Face the Nation that the Trump administration had been in touch with Nvidia’s temporary management, lead directors and lawyers while trying to find out who was in charge of compliance at the company.

“It behooves Nvidia to move ⁠quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was,” Bessent said on the program.

Kennedy, a former Louisiana state treasurer who began his political career as a Democrat before switching parties and becoming a staunch Trump administration ally, delivers many of the colloquialisms that have become his calling card with a southern US drawl.

Many believe Kennedy resorts to the drawl to come off as folksy – while he holds degrees from Vanderbilt University, the University of Virginia School of Law and the UK’s Oxford University, and is estimated to be one of the wealthiest US senators.

stories.title: My approach to EU is pragmatic, says Burnham
stories.summary: The prime minister also said his predecessors who have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate are "stuck in the past".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Burnham made the comments while addressing MPs in parliament on Monday

Published 23 November 2026

The prime minister has said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything", as he outlined his agreement with the bloc to MPs.

Andy Burnham told the Commons there was "no fixed destination" on talks to explore closer ties with the European Union, adding it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.

After several former prime ministers urged him to not reopen the Brexit debate, Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" - and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015".

At a summit on Friday, Burnham agreed a new deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

He also finalised the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU and said both sides will "brainstorm" options for their long-term relationship.

He has previously suggested potential options for the future could include rejoining the customs union, the single market or a fresh referendum on full EU membership.

However, he has ruled out major changes to the UK-EU relationship before the next general election, saying he will stick to Labour's 2024 manifesto pledge not to return to the single market, customs union or freedom of movement.

Speaking in the Commons on Monday, Conservative MP Sir Edward Leigh said the "reset" with the EU is "a prelude to the prime minister's sincere desire to rejoin the EU and have another referendum" and risked leading to another Scottish independence referendum.

Burnham replied to the Gainsborough MP: "It's not a prelude to anything. It's a pragmatic approach and it will continue to be a pragmatic approach.

"If it's in Britain's national interest, I will recommend it to this House. If it is not, then I won't. There is no fixed opinion here. There is no fixed destination.

"Europe could change again in the next year, 18 months, and we'll have to obviously watch how life changes. But where Britain can make progress, surely we should make progress."

'No banging on about Europe'

The prime minister also told MPs the government's forthcoming 10-year plan for the country will consider the "range of options for our long-term relationship with our largest market" - the EU.

MPs heard the "plan for Britain" will be published next month and the results of the "informal exchanges of ideas" with the EU will be presented around the time of their next joint summit.

To laughter from the opposition benches, Burnham said: "So there will be no banging on about Europe from this side or a running commentary."

The words echoed those used by Conservative former Prime Minister Lord Cameron in 2006 .

Burnham went on to say there would be a "calm, constructive and pragmatic consideration of what is in Britain's interests in the long-term", adding "always the British people will be the boss and they will decide what comes next".

Conservative MP Sir Bernard Jenkin asked Burnham to "give a clear and unequivocal statement that it would be unthinkable for any prime minister to try and take the UK back into the EU without a referendum".

Burnham replied to the Harwich and North Essex MP : "Yes, it would be unthinkable."

Theresa May 'aghast' at Burnham's EU plans and says 'Brexit is done' Published 1 day ago

'Move on!' Former PMs pile in with advice for Andy Burnham, but will he listen? Published 1 day ago

Speaking for the Opposition, Badenoch said Burnham's EU deal "wasn't really about reducing the cost of living" but instead "committing Britain to becoming a rule taker from Brussels, something he had no mandate to do".

Badenoch also said: "Six former prime ministers, including Tony Blair, are criticising the direction he is taking UK-EU relations. He says the prime ministers who implemented a democratic decision are living in the past.

"The only person living in the past is the man trying to take Britain back to 2015 instead of focusing on the future."

Over the weekend, Baroness May, who spent three years negotiating an EU exit deal, told the BBC she was "aghast" Burnham could be considering rejoining.

She urged him to "accept Brexit and move on".

Rishi Sunak has also warned against reopening the "divisive" debate about rejoining the EU, telling Sky News it would be "a huge distraction for government".

Earlier this month, Boris Johnson, who negotiated the original Brexit deal as prime minister, said it was "madness" for Burnham to make Brexit his "political priority".

He told the Daily Telegraph , external , he believed the public would back Brexit again if Burnham forced another vote on the issue.

His predecessor Lord Cameron, who resigned as prime minister after losing the 2016 Brexit referendum, has also warned against "another-decade long debate about whether we should be in or out".

Meanwhile, former Labour Prime Minister Sir Tony - who was a prominent opponent of leaving the EU - has said the UK should only rejoin the bloc if it reforms and allows more innovation on technology.

Asked about the criticism from his predecessors, Burnham earlier told broadcasters: "They're stuck in the past because they can't face up to the bad deal that they did."

He added: "I'm not a prime minister that's going to be stuck in the past."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey welcomed the new agreements before telling the Commons that a "totally new deal for Britain" is needed now.

Reform UK deputy leader Richard Tice labelled it a "terrible" deal, while Green Party MP Ellie Chowns said "bold and brave politics, not baby steps" are needed.
